Blest are those docile ones; they are those .9 whom God selects to work for Him. - PERFECT DRESS.—The primary objects of dress are, I imagine, first, to afford a general protection to the body, and, secondly, to maintain it everywhere at a proper and equame temperature. To these two purposes must be lour Worship, to circulation." 1 , I think of death as the first Pulse of the new strength Ahaking itself free from the old mouldy remnants of rth garments, that it may begin in freedom the new life , ',that grows out of the old.—Macdonald. , How often do we look upon God as our last and 'feeblest resource. We go to Him because we have no- where else to go. And then we learn that the storms of *life have driven us, not upon the rocks, but unto the 'desired haven.—ffaedonald. , Not unblest is he who sees; added a third for which, however, but a minor import- ' ance can he claimed: the purpose, namely, of dress to act as a vehicle for personal decoration and ornament. The first two of these objects express in a general man- ner the relations of dress to health; the third concerns solely the decorative attributes of clothing. In all criticisms that are passed upon dress from a hygienic or utilitarian point of view these primary objects must be prominently put forth. They must form a standard by which various costumes and articles of apparel can be f judged and compared; and they should form the basis lof our conception of that nebulous entity—a perfect s Shadows of God's realities; ' dress. div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 11, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JULY 11, 1885.
'NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI.
CULTURY, to,

Butter should always be churned several degrees colder in summer than in winter. The reason is that the casein- ous matter of milk more readily attaches itself to the butter globules in summer than in winter, and that this adhesion can best be prevented by a cooler temperature of the cream when churning. IMPORTED MANUE.E.—The importations of guano and phosphatic manures at the port of Cherbourg increased from 906,975 kilos in 1833 to 7,443,600 kilos in 1884, this increase being largely due, to the arrival of some big English vessels with guano from the Lobos Islands. In France, according to a consular report just issued, the use of these manures is steadily increasing. Pure bred cows are not desirable in large dairies, that is to say, they should not, if kept, form any considerable portion of it. It is generally understood that a few of the Channel Islands breeds should be in every dairy where butter is the main product, as the quality of the article is very much enhanced by the superior richness and flavour of the cream. Jerseys and Guernseys, however, are essentially butter-producing cows, and on this ac- count have a particular value, but in extensive dairying, especially where the milk is sold, or cheese made instead of butter, they are quite second-rate, having regard to the amount realised from the sale of their products. RURAL NOTES—The growth of vegetation since the heavy rainfall 'a week ago has been more remarkable than during any equal period of the year. The grass lands have filled up in a marvellous manner. Pastures are well stocked with grass of a better quality than has been seen for many years past. In place of the objec- tionable weeds which followed the long train of wet seasons, we have a more herby, nutritious grass for cattle to feed upon, and everywhere one turns grass is abundant.on the pastures. Old meadow land promises to excel both in quantity and quality. The grass being quickly grown at the best period of its term is full of juice, and the weight of the crop is over the average. The northern counties have apparently fared better tor grass than the more southern districts. There is a con- siderable portion both of rye grass and clover and old meadow grass cut in the Fylde, and a good many fields have already been cleared. In every instance that I have seen the grass cuts up well. Every day will bring more people intb haymaking, and by the end of this week the work will be in full swing in all the earlier dis- tricts of Lancashire and Cheshire. In some parts of the country complaints are made that oats will be short in the straw, but I do not find any ground for these com- plaints, only in very exceptional cases. Oats have come forward very satisfactorily and.have made amends for their sickly appearance of three or four weeks ago. BEES.—THIRTY YEARS' PROGRESS.— During the Last thirty years great discoveries have been made in the natural history and general management of bees. The invention of the movableLcomb hive, introduced and improved upon by Mr. Langstroth about 1852, opened a wide field of study; in fact, it was the invention of the age as regards intelligent bee-keeping, and upon it was hinged most of the progress that has been made since. By its use we were enabled to go inside the hive and prove those things at which naturalists had hinted. It enabled us to practice artificial multiplication of swarms, or prevent natural swarming when desirable. That bees, deprived in any way of their queen, had the means to rear another one had long been known, but till now the knowledge was 'of but little practical value. Now we are enabled to rear queens at will, to become ac- quainted with their good or bad qualities and to breed and to perpetuate the one and discard the other; and also if another race of bees is thought to be superior to the ones we are breeding, the movable frame enables us to introduce foreign stock without loss. Science has also demonstrated that to elaborate and build comb causes bees much labour, and that it is at the expense of a large, quantity of honey. Take an .ordinary bee- hive of 2,000 cubic inches capacity and to fill it with nice new comb requires labour sufficient to bring in 301 b. of honey, and the elaboration of wax to form material for the building of the comb requires 301 b. more. We find that 601 b. at least of honey has been the cost of fill- ing each hive. Enterprising bee-keepers sought to obviate in that measure this outlay, and the result has been the honey extractor, whereby the newly-closed cells are uncapped, and the frames with combs attached are taken from the hive, the bees brushed off, and then placed in the machine and rapidly revolved, emptying the honey from the cells, and then the combs replaoed in the hive to be refilled, and the process repeated when advisable. Twenty years ago, had some timid apiarist ventured to suggest the possibility of making artificial comb, which the bees would readily accept and utilise the same as their own, he would have been a fit subject for a lunatic asylum; but nearly as long ago as that the embryonian idea took root in the brain of Mehring, of Germany, and later by Mr. Wagner of our country, I and the result has been the production of foundation- comb that can be attached to the frame and placed within the hive, and be as readily used by the bees for 1 all purposes as their own. These are some of the won. d rful results that have accrued by the application of certain principles in accordance with the no less won- derful instincts and habits of the honey bee.—Bee- keepers' Magazine. THE PROPER FEEDING OP HORSES.— -A writer in the American Agriculturist says :—" Condition in horses is not fat—far from it—it is hard, tough, elastic muscle, which may be actively worked without tiring the horse, without sweating, and without exhaustion of the vital forces, unless the exercise is utterly excessive. • A horse out of condition is exhausted by a half-mile trot, comes in puffing and breaks out in a sweat, while one in con- dition returns all the fresher in appearance for his blood being stirred. What 'makes the difference? Proper feeding, good grooming, and regular work or exercise, and enough of it. All exercise tires the muscles brought into play—a tired muscle needs feeding. The feed for the muscle is digested food. After any muscle has been taxed it is for some time in a condition to appropriate from the blood the proper elements to build itself up and increase its strength. When a horse is fed imme- diately before labour, the food remains undigested until labour ceases, and then is liable to do harm. All horse- men know that a horse should not have a feed of grain when warm. or until he has cooled off, yet when they I start a horse off to any kind of hard work or road work before his food has time to digest he is liable to be in- jured by it. After labour, as soon as a horse cools off and is rested, the blood, which the use of the muscles drew to the extremities, returns, and is ready to take active part in the work of digestion. Then is the time to feed. To get a horse rapidly into condition, he should be well worked or exercised according to his strength; when brought in, vigorously rubbed, and when dry, cool, and rested, fed. His food should be good hay when his appetite is sharpest, followed by oats which in quality should be unexceptionable, and in quantity gauged according to ,the work he does. Fat will sweat off, muscle will not. A fat horse is liable to in- digestion, sun-stroke, cold, flatulence (colic), and ever so many other ills, which a horse in condition is not only free from, but if properly fed, and cleaned, and worked, is not liable to get. It is usually poor economy to reduce either food or exercise. SHELTER FOR STOCK ore PASTCRE.—SheIter for live stock in winter is justly considered a most essential part of farm management, but, although such is the case, the necessity for shelter while these winter-housed stock are on the grass in summer and autumn is often neglected and considered unnecessary. A fence of any sort, suffi- cient to keep them within bounds, is generally all that is seen in many localities. Not even a clump of trees is provided, much less any other artificial mode of pre- serving the animals from the heat of summer or from cold blasts and drenching rains which are common towards the end of autumn before cattle are put into their winter quarters. The effect of heat is often seriously prejudicial to cattle which spend several hours daily racing through the fields, annoyed by insects dur- ing warm weather; it must seriously affect the progress of fattening beasts, the yield of milk of dairy stock, and. the growth of young cattle. As to dairy stock, it would be much better to keep them in the house during the hottest part of the day, even although there might be little to give them in the way of food. There is often a great waste of material in".the different stages of meat manufacturer:which might be remedied by providing shelter; and it need scarcely be said that everything Ivhich causes waste of material results in a certain amount of loss to the stockowner. A considerable por- tion of the food being expended in maintaining the na- tural heat of their bodies, it is apparent that, if fatten- ing cattle fare exposed to low temperature and chills, either their progress must be retarded or an additional expenditure of food incurred.' Besides, exposure to cold winds and too much wet is liable to bring on lung dis- ease or rheumatic complaints, which are not easily got rid of, if they do not end seriously. Sheds can easily be erected in pasture fields, at very little expense, by means of wooden posts and sides, covered over with straw or brushwood. Felt or prepared canvas, coated with tar, or Willisden paper, are also cheap and convenient modes of covering. Sheds in pasture fields may be useful in winter as well as summer. Cattle soon learn to use them when they have free ingress or egress; and a con- siderable quantity of manure might be collected in them at little trouble or expense. Want of shelter may be considered no small evil; on the contrary, it has been frequently known to have been productive of serioua consequences.

One half the world doesn't know how the other half lives. It is just as well. It saves a great deal of gassip. A lady, with a sigh, exclaimed, "Well, I have lost my lawsuit!' "Oh, mamma! how glad I am," said her child, "that you have lost it, for it tormented you awfully." "There are good and bad points about this coffee," said the American boarder in a judicial tone. "The good Point is that there is no chicory in it; the bad, that there is no coffee in it!"

COTTAGE GARDENING STRAWBERRIES.—The first indications of ripening were observed on the 26th ult. on some keen seedling, on a south border a few miles south-east of Preston, so we may expect to hear of a few being picked in the open, in favoured localities in this district, by the time these lines appear, if the weather continues sunny. It is most essential to top dress the surface of the soil between the rows, so as to prevent the finer particles of soil being j washed on to the fruit, which would render it almost t worthless. The materials in general use are short litter, , spent tan, short grass, and spent hops. Those who may I only have a few roots will find it an excellent plan to support the fruit with a few forked sticks, which will j also help to preserve them from slugs, which are sure Ito attack the figest fruit. So far as we have seen there is a promise of a heavy crop, the rain that fell more than , a week ago coming just in time to swell it to its utmost j capacity. APPLES AND PEARS.—The same rainfall washed our fruit trees, and ievealed to us the exact state of things. The ground was literally covered with small pears, which no doubt had been crippled by the continuous cold winds during May. Some of the hardier kinds have a fair sprinkling on them, and some of the choicest sorts that have the protection of a wall are in some in- stances well-loaded with fruit. At Worden Hall, Ley- land, we learn that some of the varieties on the walls were so thick that a dozen might be covered with the hand. Apples are as well cropped as the most greedy could desire. We prefer the crop we have to the one that was anticipated. Extra heavy crops, as the apple promised to be, are productive of little good to any one. In the first instance, it is generally followed by a season of unusual scarcity, and the fruit on the heavily laden trees is usually small. The grower also finds that it does not pay him to gather the fruit and convey it any great distance to market; so that 'only those who are near enough to fetch the fruit derive any benefit. Dwellers in towns are, as a rule, some miles from orchard gardens, and however bountiful the crop may be, we, find they have to pay about the same as when the produce is moderate. CHERRIES are a good average crop, and the Morello is perfectly loaded. This is the variety so highly esteemed for making cherry brandy, and there is none to equal it for culinary purposes. The sweet cherries are colouring fast, and they need careful watching, or the birds will take them as fast as they show their red tints. When the trees are against a building, protection is easily supplied by suspending a net in front of the trees. THE FRONT GARDEN.—During the operation of plant- ing out in the beds or borders there is always more or less treading of the surface of the soil, and the more in- experienced the operator may be the less command will he have over his feet. They are so restless that they must be perpetually moving, till every patch of bare sur- face has the print of a shoe, and finally their unfortu- nate owner becomes oblivious of their presence, and for want of sufficient space between the plants many have had the life crushed out of them. The experienced planter will plant a bed 4ft. in diameter without mak- ing feet marks' providing he can get round it. If the space is wider he will first fix his foot at a certain point, and will plant all that is required within a radius of 18 inches from the toes of his outstretched foot before moving it, and when he has finished he carefully forks the soil and, if necessary, fills the space with plants. These depressions, beside being unsightly, act adversely on the plants in more viays than one, and they should be raised by the fork or spade. The whole surface of the flower beds should have the Dutch hoe run over every vacant part so as to destroy the weeds as well as to maintain a porous surface. The appearance of the plants will also be improved if all decayed leaves and flowers are removed as they appear. Dahlias i Cottagers, ' as a rule, have to plant old roots, and some of them throw up as many as half -a-dozen shoots, which are too many to be supported by the roots or to be tied to a ' single stake. It is best to reduce them to three by mov- ing the weakest. ' THE WiNnow.—Plants in boxes must be daily exa- mined as to watering lest they become dry and receive a check. When water is applied, sufficient should be given to soak all the soil. Plants of a creeping nature that may be in the boxes should have timely support if it is intended to train them round the window. There should for this purpose be inserted in the box a sound stake about a foot long to maintain the • plant steady at the base, but higher up string will answer the purpose, and this can be secured at the bottom to the box or nails may be driven into the joints of the bricks.

CRUSHED TO DEATH BY A HORSE.—On Sunday Morning a waggonette with three horses left Shaw, near Oldham, for Rippouden, driven by John Henry Ashton, aged 20. When near Saddleworth the horses took fright in going down an incline. Ashton did his best to pull up, bat the reins broke and got entangled in the horses' legs. The animals fell, and Ashton fell from his box between them, the horses treading on him and crushing his head. He was picked up dead. The waggonette was upset and four of its occupants were injured, but not seriously. .tURRIETERS—wbose professional labours necessitate long In. tervals between meals—nothing will be found so exhilarating. comforting, and capable of sustaining exhausted tature as Cadbury's Cocoa, guaranteed absolutely pure.—. IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT-

. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Motemer. The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 3 45. Naw PEERS =The Dui of Iddesleigh (sir S. Northcote), Who eras introduced by Earl Beauchamp and the Earl Of Devon; Lord Ashbourno (Mr. Gibson), introduced by the ,Earl of Longford and Lord Ventry •, and Lord St. Oswald (Mr. Be Winn), introduced by Lord Barrington andiLord Cloncurry, took the eath and subscribed the roll, on their elevation. Several bills were advanced a stage without discussion. STATEMENT BY THE PREMIER. The Marquis ef Settfoeueir, arising amid cheer., in mov- ing the adjournment of the House, made a statement as to the intentions of the Government, more particularly in re- gard to foreign affairs. The first matter was the negotia- tion with Russia respecting the Afghan frontier. The first 4 duty of the Government was to see that the pledges which the English Government had given were observed. The Chief difference between England and Russia related to the Zulficar Pass. England had/ promised the Ameer this Pms shall be included in Afghan territory, and it was of high and vital importance that we should let it be thoroughly known that the word of England once given Will be sustained and adhered to. (Cheers.) This promise, however, given to the Ameer, was only consequent upon another promise given by Russia, that the Zulficar Pass Should be included in the territory of the Arneer. Differ- ences had arisen as to the precise application of those pre - misses, and those differences were now the subject of nego- tiations. Mier as he had had an opportunity of judging, ,thee were conducted lay both Courts with au earnest desire to arrive at an amicable settlement. The other matter to be dealt with was the question of Egypt. In that country her Majesty's Government kad to deal with one of the most complicated and entangled of problems, and the conclusion bad beec arrived at that the most important consideration that should be kept before our minds was so to weigh our -steps as that when once taken they should not have to be retraced. Then came the political difficulty, which was Perhaps greater than the military. Vast tetritories in the Soudan which were under the government of Egypt had ceased to be so. They had been desolated, and every ves- tige of progress stamped out, and the population reduced tO a miserable phantom of its former strength; and yet We could not abaudon these provinces to their fate. There Was the question—How muck of the Soudan ought to re- Main under the Government of Egypt? There was the further question—How much beyond that ought to be so far under the military control of Egypt that attack from forces in the desert shall no longer be feared? Those ques- tions most be solved before we could say we had placed Er.tvpt in sufficient security, or before we have paideoff the debt which our past intervention had created. The ques- tion of finance was really of the first importance. Until that was settled nothing could be &me. The next point Was to make the frontier safe from barbarous enemies, and to fix the political relations of Egypt to the vast territories already referred to. We had bad to deal with the Khe- dive who had shown himself loyal and steadfast in the highest degree, and whom we were bound to support. With repect to domestic affairs it was said that a nation that has no history is happy, and he (the noble Marquis) hoped England will be happy during the next few weeks. The Peculiar circumstances of the case seem to prescribe to the Government the ayoidance of all attempts at legislation on Which contention would arise, and the necessity of cenfiniwg themselves to the paseing of necessary measures, and bringing the session as soon as possible to a close. He saw that in some quarters it Was supposed that there was a dark design on his part to push off the dissolution in order that the present Government may enjoy as long as possible what aome people were pleased to call the sweets of office." There was no foundation for those rumours. After taking Counsel with Earl Kimberley they came to the conclusion that November 17th'was the earliest date which they could confidently count on for the dissolution. That was forecasting a long way ahead, but certainly no one could be more desirous than the Government to bring the present anomalous state of affairs to a close, and assuredly there Would be no delay at their hands. ((Theers.) The Earl of CARNARVON stated the general position of the Government with regard to Irish affairs. In theweears 1880, 1881, and 1882, the number of agrarian crimes in Ire- land rose to 3,580 in 1880, 4,439 in 1881, and 3,433 in 1882. In 1883, after the passing 'of the Crimes Act, they fell tei 70, and last year they only numbered 762. Last year there „ewati no case of the worst form of crime—actual murder. Whereas agrarian crime rose in the three ye ire to an enor- Mous extent, it has since fallen below the level of the years Prior to 1880. It was impossible to conceive a graver matter on Which A Government could he called to deliberate within a 1-,ery short time, when the Crimes Act would expire. Since 1847 Ireland had been almost constantly under exceptional Ingislatioe, That state of things was not satisfactory. When the existing legislation against crime was enacted, raffia- tuent intended that it should come to an end in three years. . At had produced the desired effects, and as there was now So extraordinary crime in Ireland Her Majesty's Govern- Meat proposed te govern that country by administering the ordinary law firmly and effectively; and in undertaking the office of Viceroy, he did not despair of seeing that on the one side there would be good feeling towards England, and On the other good government of Ireland. Be!Lerd KIMBERLEY, while concurring generally with the rrernier'a remarks as to the Afghan frontier and Egypt, thought that the noble lord rather overestimated the power fief the Mandi. Having observe that it was very unusual ler a,Lord Lieutenant to make a statement of pelicy, he Rated that he viewed with apprehension the experiment the %vernment were about to make in Ireland. The late Go- Vern went tried it, and it was a failure. The Dram of ARGYLL thought that there was nothing ,to Complain of in the speeches delivered from the front Peaches, which were of an academic character. He would, however, on Friday call attention to recent political Went.. T.h, 111 The '-1110 Of ROSEBERY, in reference to a remark made 1-7 t'dt .. 3 t inarquis of Salisbury, said he intended to bring in irneenediately the Secretary for Scotland Bill. Their lordships rose at 6-20. HOUSE OF COMMONS—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 4.0. NEw WRITS —On the motion of Mr. AKERS-DOUGLAS, a 'eel,' writ was issued for Brighton, in the room of Mr. Mar- nott. who has accepted the office of Judge Advocate- teetteral.—A new writ was also issued for Chatham, in the roota of Mr. Garet, who has accepted the office of Solicitor- General. TER RE-ELECTED MINISTERS, all of whom were warmly Welcomed, took the oath and their seats On re-election. , NEW MEMBER.—Mr. Green, who was introduced by Sir Hay and Sir F. Milner, took the oath and his seat for Iyakefield. MR. terms. If it were carried, he should move to limit it to Parliamentary oaths and to this particular case. The MITORNEY-GENERAL argued that the amendment resolved itself into a Bradlaugh Relief Bill, and nothing more. Sir H. JAMES asked, if the question was not a religious one, what was it? The Howse had refused tp allow Mr. Bradlaugh to affirm, and it was, therefore, necessary that they.should adopt legislation to remove that which preven- ted persons from affirming and prevented constituencies being represented by those who desired to affirm rather than to take the oath. Mr. LABorcermas insisted that as Mr. 13radlaugh had acted in a conciliatory manner, the House ought to meet him in the same conciliatory spirit.--Mr. MITCHELL HENRY protested against the literature disseminated by the hon. member for Northampton. but would vote for the amendment for the benefit of those who conscientiously ob. j .cted to call upon the. Deity to witness an oath.—Mr. COURTNEY spoke in favour of the amend ment.-----Mr. WAL- TER maintained that the best settlement was to allow those who desired it to affirm ;' and after some remarks from Mr. Storer Mr: A. Balfour. and Mr. Newdegate the House divided, and Mr. Hopwood's amendment was nega- tived by 263 to 219. On the Chancellor of the Exchequer's resolution being put as the substantive motion, Mr. Gladstone said that, as on previous occasions, be should offer no opposition. Mr. Labouchere and Mr. Willis; however, declared that they would divide against it; but when the House had been cleared they would allow the resolution to be carried without a division. Mr. Bradlaugh then advanced to the table, standing face to face with the Speaker. The SPEAKER : I call upon you to withdraw. Mr. BRADLAnoIi : I am here, sir, in obedience to the wish of my constituents. 1 submit to your direction to with- draw, appealing to the constituencies against the injustice done. (Cheers from the Opposition benches.) Mr. Bradlaugh then quitted the Huse. The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER stated that Lord Harrowby had accepted the office of Lord Privy Seal with- out a ealavy. THE BUSINESS OF THE SESSIONS. In answer to Mr. Collings, who asked what facilities the Government were Prepared to afford for the consideration of tho Medical Relief Bill, the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said he proposed to make a statement next day as to legislation during the remainder of the session, which, he eaid,the Governenent desired to bring to a close as speedily as pos- sible. • SUPPLY.—The House then west into Committee of Sup- ply, and wig engaged until a late hour in consideration of the Civil Servias Estimates, Class 11. (Salaries and .Ex- pensai of Civil Depart rnenre). Class V. was also completed, and the Chairman at this point left the chair. .THE EAST INDIA'LOAN BILL Was named. through Com- mittee, and after some further business had been disposed of the House adjourned at 1-25. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 0 o'clock. itattwaa s,AND CartaLs.—On the order for the second reading of the Regent's Canal City and Docks Railway Bill, the Earl of RAVRNSWORTH proposed that in respect` of that measure the Standing Order which prohibited the pay- ment of interest of capital during construction should be suspended.--Earl SRLBDRNE said the Standing Order seemed to rest upon exceedingly sound principles. Men should not be deluded into the idea that they were receiving interast when they were only getting back their money--The Marquis of SALISBURY, remarking that the question was not one of party, was unable to take the view which had been expressed by Lord Sel borne. He viowed with some alarm the tendency to make the Standing Orders of the House of Commons laws of the Modes and Persians which Were never to be relaxed.---The Earl of WEstrss defended the Standing Order.--The Earl of KIMBRRLEY reminded the House that in 1883 Lord Salisbury spoke in defence of the Standing Order which it was now proposed to set aside. Nothing could be worse than to have Stand- ing Orders for the protection of the public' and then to set, them aside in a particular case because 'a little popularity was to be got by so doing. (Cheers.)--The House divi- ded, and the motion was carried by 46 to 37.—The bill was read a second time.
The Friendly Societies Act (1875) Amendment Bill pas- sed through committee, and the House rose at 6-10.. HOUSE OF COMMONS.--Tuuswa. . . . .

• The Speaker took the chair shortly before 4-0. An hour's discussion took place on a motion by Mr, RAIKES IO refer back the Dee Conservancy Bill to the com- mittee on Standing Orders, the committee having reported in respect to the Bill that the Standing Orders were not complied with. On a division, the inotion was rejected by 155 to 129. QUESTIONS, &C. —On the motion of Lord RICEIARD GROSVENOR a new writ was ordered to issue for Aylesbury in the place of Sir Nathaniel de Rothschild, who becomes a 'peer.—ln reply to Dr: Cameron, Lord Joust MANHEres an- nounced that it is not the intention of the Government to proceed with the measure for the introduction of sixpenny telegrams.—ln reply to Mr. Cavendish Bentinct, who was much cheered on rising to sec a question relating to the publication of certain articles in an evening paper, Sir IL R. CROSS guardedly answered that means existed of sub- jecting the authors and publishers to criminal proceedings, but it remained with a jury to decide the measure of guilt. —ln reply to Mr. McLaren, Sir M. H. BEAM said the ar- rangements for the mission of Sir H. Wolff to Egypt had not been determined upon. It was true the right hon. mem- ber had been a director of two financial companies connected, with Egypt, but one was long deceased, and from the other he had retired. There was nothing in his public action which to Sir M. H. Beach seemed to debar him from under- taking the special mission referred to. Sir Michael's ex- pression of opinion that Sir Henry Wolff" would be accept- a'ale at the Khedive'e Court " excited much laughter.—Mr. McLABEN gave notice to move a resolution declaring that Sir Henry Wolff is not a desirable person to undertake a commission to Egypt, and will ask what facilities the Go- vernment will provide for discussing the motion.—Mr. W. H. SMITH informed Si, John Hay that it was his intention to propose a vote of thanks to the forces who have served in the Soudan and on the Nile —ln reply to Sir H. Selwin- Ibbetson, Sir R. Cnoss said it was impossible to go on with the Police Superannuation Bill, and he would therefore move its discharge. PUBLIC BUSINESS.—GOVERNMENT STATEMENT. _

_ At half-past five Sir M.H. Beach rose to make the promieed statement with respect to the business of the Session. The object of the Government was, he said, to wind up the busi- ness of the Session as soon as possible, and take the earliest , opportunity of appealing to the constituences. The main , business that remaieed to the Government was to complete , Votes in Supply and Ways and Means. With respect to , Bills, it was their intention to find an opportunity of laying , their views with respect to land purchase in Ireland before Patliament. If they found opposition in the way they would not press the measure. With respect to the Coercion Bill, Mr. Gladstone had announced the intention of the late Government te renew certain "valuable and teplitable pro- , visions "of the Crimes Act. Bat Sir Michael announced, , amid laughter and cheers from the Ministerial aid!, the new Government could find no trace of the preperation of any such Bill. He, however, did not mention that by way of / complaint, as the Government did not propose to renew the , Act. This announcement, for which the House was well , prepared, was received with demonstration. But Sir Michael, proceeding to state that this decision was taken because the Conservative Government " objected to exceptional I legislation of this character," there followed from e the Liberal side a prolonged burst of laughter. When he found opportunity Sir Michael added, " unless , such legislation is clearly necessary for the preservation of order." There was more laughter when the Chancellor of , the Exchequer proceeded to state that since the change of Government had taken place there was evidence of a better I feeling in Ireland. As to other bills, he could not bold out any hope of proceeding with the Crofters Bill nor with the Welsh Education Act. With respect to this last there was another outburst of laughter when he proceeded gravely to , declare that the Government would devote their best atten- tion to the matter during the autumn, "and if it should be , our good fortune—" be continued; but here the laughtlr came in with such force that the sentence remained un- / finished. He also undertook to find opportunity for a de. , elevation of the opinion of the House on the subject of the Medical Relief Disqualificatien Bill. The Government • were also in favour of passing into law some of the provisions of the Criminal Law Amendment Bill. On this subject he would confer with Sir W. Harcourt. (Cheers.) Mr. GLADSTONE, on rising, was much cheered from the Liberal side. The cheers were taken up by the Conserva- tives when the Leader of thee Opposition declared that he would not be able to &ippon 'Sir W. Lawson's amendment, at the same time, amid general applause, congratulating the hon. baronet upon his recovered health. Touching upon foreign matters, Mr. Gladstone announced that in the nego- tiations with the late Government Russia had undertaken to make over to the Ameer of Afghanistan the Pass of Zultikar. He asserted that as far as the action of the new Government was directed towards brining about a peaceful and honour- able settlement of the difficulty with Russia, they would receive the support of himself and his colleagues. He spoke amid Conservative cheering in the seine conciliatory spirit on the subj,ct of Egypt. He expressed regret that the Government did not see their way to deal with the Crofters Bill, he himself regarding; legislation on that point as urgent for the peace of the country. He reserved dis- cretion to himself and his friends to consider the matter further. He accepted the decisicat about the Welsh Educa- tion Bill, and frankly adrnittel that the Government pro- posed to deal with the Medical Relief fill and the Criminal Ls* Amendment Bill in a liberal spirit. He presumed that no snbetantial change:would be made in the provisional ar- rangement entered into for the suspension of the Con- tagious Diseases Act, and concluded a most conciliatory speech by heartily wishing success to the new Government. (Cheers.) Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL thanked Mr. Gledstone for his "considerate and magnanimous treatment of the pro- posals of the Government."—ln reply to Mr. Stanefeld, Mr. W. H. SMITH gave an aseurance that the Government would not interfere with the course taken with respect to the Con• tagieue Diseases Act. THE VOTE or CENSURE —By this time the House had dwindled to the lowest point of attendance, and Sir W. LAWSON, with a very scanty audience, moved his amend- that the Hones had no confidence in thi Gmenv r dnculeanrti and could not therefore appropriate to there oer:R the time asked for by Sir Michael Hicks-Beach.—Later, Mr. LEWIS introduced some liveliness into the fagged debate by 1 a vigorous attack on the Government for their decision in I respect of the Crimes Act.—Mr. Ktero-Hattetaer heroically declared that if the Crimes Act were allowed to lapse he would go and live among his tenants.—Sir FARRER.IIER.

C actual., in a lively speech, expressed the satisfaction with which on the Liberal side they had heard speeches from members opposite. The Conservatives at the end of six years Conservative rule had declared it would be criminal not to pees a Coerciou Bill. Al the end of five years of Liberal rule they protested that it would be c. 'millet to renew the Act.—On a division Sir Wilfrid Lawson's amend- ment was rejected by 151 votes against two. the minority being composed of Mr. Briggs and Mr. Carbutt. PRINCESS BEATRICE'S MARRIAGE PORTION.—Tbe House then went into Committee of Supply, whereupon the CHAN- CELLOR OE THE EXCHEQUER moved a greet of £30,000 to Her Royal Highness the Princess Beatrice as a provision on her forthcoming marriage. The right hon. gentleman expressed a hope that the vote would not meez with any opposition on the present occasion.—Mr. LABOUCIIERE ex- pressed his intention to oppose the vote as one which was un- necessary in view of the lance accumulations of property which had fallen to her Majesty, the ohject of which was to enable her to make necessary provision to maintain her own family.—On a division there were for the vote 153, against 32. The House adjourned at half-past two o'clock on Wed- nesday morning. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at a quarter after twelve o'clock. DURHAM SUNDAY CLOSING BILL. —• On the motion of Mr. AKERS DOUGLAS, the order for the second reading of the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sunday (Durham) Bill was read and discharged, and the Bill was withdrawn. Vice.AentniAL HOBART.—L3rd G. HAMILTON, replying to Sir G Campbell, stated that Vice-Admiral Hobart Harlin- den ( Hobart Pasha) WAS removed from the naval list in 1868 in cous«peence of his baying accepted an appointment in the Turkish service. In 1874 he was reinstated, but again in 1877 his name was removed when war broke out between Turkey and Russia. The late Government had been pleased to accede to the request of the Admiral to place his name upon the list of retired naval officers, this having been done by an Order in Council of June 24, 188.5. The noble lord asserted that he had no evidence to support the assumption of Sir G. Campbell that during the greater part of his service the Admiral had been engaged in other pursuits, some of them in contravention of the laws of this country and of the laws of nations. NAVAL ESTIMATES.—The House went into Committee of Supply on the Navy Estimates, and Sir J. Hey called at- tention to the tate of the navy, and condemned the Evolu- tionary Squadron under Admiral Hoskins as wholly un- suited to such special service as that upon which it was engaged. Sir E. Reed also strongly condemned the char- acter of the Evolutionary Squadron in Bantry Bay, which, be said, had recently been intended for the Baltic. but was totally unfit for that service. Lord G. Hamilton remarked that the Board of Admiralty felt that they had to proceed upon estimates of their predecessors, but their object would be to place the navy in as efficient a state as possible. A short discussion followed, in which tee transport service was criticised, and Lord G. Hamilton promiaed tnat a thorough investigation should be made in the matte r. Atten- tion was called to the state of the intelligence department and the Volunteer movement in its connection with coast- guard service, estuary defence was considered; and some remarks were made by hon. members on the policy of the present Board of Admiralty in regard to shipbuilding. • Mr. Labouchere's motion to reduce the vote for the Royal yacht Victoria and Albert was defeated by 128 to 37. On the vote for retired pay Sir G. Catnpbell moved to ,reduce it by £284, the amount of retired pay to Hobart Pasha, rand protested against the reinstatement of that officer as a distinct reversal of the decision of the Government in 1877. After the subject had been discussed for some time it was discovered that the vote did not include the grant in question, and, the vote having been agreed to, progress was reported. The East India Loan Bill was read a third-time, one or two meesnres were ad- vanced a stage, and leave was given to bring in some new bills, one being for complete enfranchisement of the con- stabulary forces of the United Kingdom. The Committee on Forestry having been nominated, the order of the day re- lating to the Merchant Shipping (Transfer of Registry) Bill was discharged, and the bill was withdrawn. The House adjourned at ten minutes to six. HOUSE OF LORDS.—lMuresuar. I _

_ The Lord Chancellor toOk his seat on the woolsack at a quarter before four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS—Lord Rothschild took the oath and subscribed the roll of Parlitiment on his elevation to the peerage.—The second reading of the Secretary for Scotland Bill was moved by the Earl of BOSEBERY, who explained that it would commit to the new Secretary the charge of law and justice in Scotland. the Keepership of the Great Seal of Scotland, and the care of education in that country.—Atter remarks from several Scotch peers' the Marquis of Sells. BURY stated that if the bill passed their Lordebips' House it would be introduced in the other House as a Government measure.—The bill WAS read a second time.—The Duke of MARLBOROUGH moved the second readine of the Real Property Registration Bill, which was opposed by the Lord Caszectexrant, who pointed out that it was full of conten- tious clauses and contained no fewer than 117 sections Lord SELBORNE declared himself opposed to the bill, and the motion for second reading was withdrawn. Their Lordships adjourned at a quarter to seven o'clock.

QUESTIONS.—The Cwascsixow of the EXCHEQUER an- nouncid that the Government had resolved ..upon an inquiry into the depression of trade and industry.—Mr. BOURKE stated that it would not be conducive to the interests of the public service to produce at present the correspondence with Sir P. Lumsden.—ln reply to the question of Mr. M'Coan as to an insulting reference made by Lord R. Churchill to the Irish party in a speech at Edinburgh. the BECRRTARY for INDIi said he thought he should be abusing a privilege if be entered into a controversy at question time as to any speech he might have made some time ago. He believed that what he had said was perfectly justified by the circum- stances of the date and by the amount of information be might have had at that time at his command. TORY FINANCE —A BORROWING BUDGET.

- - _ Sir M. HICKS-BELCH presented a supplementary finer). I chi statement. He said he intended to adopt the increased taxation proposed by the late Chancellor of the Exchequer and already sanctioned, but he had not been able to satisfy himself that it was his duty under present circumstances to move for any additional taxation upon articles of con- sumption. He proposed to take the income tax at Bd. and the.increased stamp duties, bat it would be necessary to supply the deficiencies caused by the rejection of the pro- posed increase of the succession, beer, and spirit duties, which might be set down at £2650000. As to the v,te of credit for £11,000,000, the explctation of the late Chan- cellor of the Exchequer would not be realised The army expenditure on that account would not be exceeded, but it was diff,o-ent with respect to the naval exoenditure. The amount allotted to the navy wis £2 800 000, but that had already been exceeded by £B5OOOO. The wit de dtficit was practically £3,877,000. He did not propose to inteifere with the sinking fund for next year,as the Governmeat was decidedly of opinion that it ought to be left to the new Par- liament to decide whether the fund should be farther inter• fered with, and also on what principles the deicitoccasioned by the decision of the 9th of June should be met. In the meantime he proposed to meet the deficiency by the issue of Treasury or Exchequer Bills to an amount not exceeding £1 000,000. These proposals be made from a desire to in- terfere as little as possible with the trade and industry of .the country. The right hon. gentleman added that he bad ascertained that owing to the repayment of Exchequer leans the Exchequer balances on the 31st of March next were likely to be in a very favourable condition.—Mr. CHILDERS said the statement of the increased expenditure of £B3OOOO under the Vote of Credit had come upon him as a surprise, because be had taken extreme care in examining the estimates and verifying the figures. The late Govern- ment took power to deal with the wine duties, and he wished to know if the Chancellor of the Exchequer proposed to give up that power.—Sir M. fitexs-Bsecti replied that he did.—Mr. CHILDERs said the Postmaster General hinted at the abandonment of the Sixpenny Telegrams Bill, and asked if any allowance had been made for that.—Mr. W. FOWLER asked for a statement of intentions with regard to the taxation of corporate property.—Mr. H. FOWLER contended that for national expen-liture industry was over- taxed, whereas property did not bear an adequate share of the burden, and that in adjusting taxation as between pro- perty and industry they oueht to give an advantage to in- dustry, which had no reserve fund to fall back upon.—The discussion was continued by Mr. Caine and other hon. members.—Mr. ARNOLD gave notice of his intention to en- I pose that part of the Chancellor of the Exchequer's scheme I in which he adopted the proposals of hie predecessor with regard to corporate lands.—Sir M. theirs-Baader, in his I reply, referred to a suggestion of Sir W. Harcmirt that the object of the Government in proposing an inquiry into the state of trade was to establish a basis for a return to protec- tion. He entirely repudiated that interpretation. In eeti- mating the deficit he had not made any allowance for the abandonment of the sixpenny telegrarp system, because the measure was still before the House and was under the consideration of the Government as to whether it could or could not be proceeded with. .There would be a further opportunity of discussing the tax ,on corporate property.—A resolution authorising the rais- ing of money by the issue of Exchequer Bills WAS thee passed, and Sir M. ilicks.Beach obtained leave to bring in a bill embodying the Budget resolutions already agreed to by the House.

CROSS, who remarked that the House of Lords' report and evidence.; left no doubt whatever in the minds of Her Majesty's Ministers' that a bill of this kind was impera- tively necessary, and said it was the intention of tile Gov- ernment to offer Sir W. Harcourt every facility for proceed- ing with the measure.—Mr, S. l‘lottLEY said the statements made in the Pall Hall Gazette should be investigated by Use Government. He expressed his willingness personally to join in investigating the case.—The HOME SECRETARY said he would put the Bill dokvn for Tuesday, when he would state what amendments the Government were pre- pared to adopt.—The Bill was read a second time. The Federal Council of Australasia Bill was read a second time, and the remaining orders disposed of the House ad- journed at twenty minutes to three. -

div.head: WOLSEL EY.
div.p: WOLSEL EY.

Canto, MONDAY.—Lord Wolseley Sir Redvers Buller, Lord Charles Beresford, and the Staff left Cairo this even- ing for England. The station was crowded. A guard of honour of the 42nd Regiment was present. Egyptian troops were assembled outside. Lord Wolseley has transfared the • c ief command' of the British force in Egypt to Lieut.- General Sir. F. Stephenson.

DONGOLA, SIINDLY.—Dougala is completely evacuated. The rear guard, under the command of General Brackenbury, is now on its way to Lower Egypt. Mahmoud Salaar, the acting Mudir, accompanied the troops. The administration of the province has been handed over to Tumbal Herold, a d.scendant of the Kings of Argo Island, who has accepted the post of Governor. Nearly 13,000 refugees have now left for Lower Egypt. THE RUMOURED DEATH OF OLIVER PAIN.

PARIS, SaTortney.—A despatch received here from Cairo rates that, according to information which has reached the French Consulate in that city, nothing positive is Known about the fate of M. Oliver Pain. All,the tamoura respect- ing the part he is stated to have played at the camp of the Mandi, and the circumstances of his supposed death are without real foundation. EGYPTIAN FINA.NCES.
Canto, MONilia.—The hinds at the disposal of the Egyp- tian Government are only sufficient to pay their employee until the end of August.

ALEXANDRIA, SUN"DaY.—Sorne British sabjocts called a meeting at the Bourse to-day, at the close of which a tele- gram was despatched to Lord Salisbury, eoliciting in urgent t.!rms payment of the indemnities. It was also resolved to draw up a petition to his Lordship. RUSSIA AND AFGHANISTAN.

NEILS HERiT, JUNE 29,(vra Balasirsn, JuLT 2).—The RllB- - have to face at Penj,leb g more formidable enemy than the Afghans. Sickness is rife amongst the troops who are "maintaining order" in the territory, and already the mortality has been very severe. ESTAZ 'Khan, a Russianised Turcoman, who was appointed Governor of Penjdeb, is among the victims. Popular rumour here does not favour the belief that a final solution has been found for the frontier question. It is generally reported that the Russians are only waiting for the autumn to advance on Herat. Meanwhile the British mission continues its quiet work of observation and patient watchfultpss. The camp at present is pitched at a place between Ktunkh and Herat. THE ANNAMITE ATTACK ON GENIMAL COURC

NAM, Mom:ay.—et the opening of to-day's sitting of the Chamber of Deputies, G3neral Cameenon, Minister of War, read three despatches received from General de Conrcy con- cerning the Annamite attack upon the Freoch at Hue. The attack commenced at one o'clock on Sunday morning. At the same time the straw barracks, occupied by the French troops, were set on fire by rockets. All the soldiers' effects were destroyed, but the ammunition and provisions were saved. At dawn the French troops advanced against the enerny, whe are said to have numbered 30,000 men, and put them to fight. The losses of the Annamites were from 1,200 to 1,500. The losses af the French are said to have been 80 killed and wounded. After th\e reading of these telegrams Mgr. Freppel moved that the debate on the treaty of peace with China should be adjourned, as the events at Hue had, he alleged. modified the situatiora This motion was opoosed by M. de Frevcinet. Ultimately the treaty was ratified by a large majority. Pears, WEDNESDAY.—The Minister of War received to-day the following telegram from General de Courcy, dated flue, eleven o'clock last night :—" We are absolute masters here. The enemy's troops are dispersing. There have been some isolated conflagrations in the neighbourhood of the Legation building, and in certain portions of the citadel, but the Royal Palace is still intact, thanks to the exemplary discipline of the battalion of Zouaves who cap- tured the place and are now guarding it. The Palace cm- talus a great store of wealth, comprising bar silver to the value of 5,000,000 francs, which figure will b 3 largely in- creased should any gold bars be found. The artistic Fiches of the Palace are inestimable. I shall await instructions. I request authority to confer a larger number of crosses and medals than I have here available."

Perils, WEDNESDAY Evameio.—The latest telegrams from General de Courcy report that some French movable colurns are p wading the environs of line, searching for Thuyet, the Annamite Minister of War, who is the supposed prime instigator of the attack upon the French. FRANCE AND MADAGASCAR.

HURRICANE IN AUSTRIA.-FIVE TLIOUSAND PEOPLE HOAELESS. .

VIENNA, FRIDA-Y----ileaTi-ur 11—n7H-cane has tiering the past two days been raging over Bakowina and Galicia, Causing serious lose of life and immense destruction ot pro- perty. In many districts the crop has been completely destroyed by the hail, while toweships have been laid ware. Many of the fine forests of Bulowina aad Galicia have likewise sustained considerable damage. Reports from the regions over which the storm passed state that upwards of 10,000 oaks and mapiPs have been uprooted. During the height of the hurricane, a fire, supposed to have been caused by lightning, broke out at Florodenka. in Galicia, a town of some 8,000 or 9,000 inhabitants. and, aided by toe high wind, nomad with such rapidity that before it could be extinguished 600 houses had been reduced to ashes, and the poor people whom they heti sheltered, to the number of 5,000, madered homeless. These unfortunates, who are mainly Jews of the very poorest class, are now without shelter of any kind, and also almost entirely without food. Two of the inhabitants were burned to death. Subacrip- tions in aid of the suftrrers have already been opened by most of the newspapers here. GREAT FIRE IN AMERICA.

A Central News telegram, dated Paris, Toursdty noon, s ,ye :—According to an apparently authoritative announce- ment, cholera has broken out at Vigean in the Department of the Etude, which is situated on the south-east frontier of Spain. Several deaths have already occurred there. The disease is supposed to have been brought by fugitives from Spain. THE FALL OF KHARTOUM.

The Daily News says:—" The positively last ' man From Khartoum is one Abdullah Bey Is:nail, who cam- mended one of the battalions of irregular troops at the siege of that place, and who escaped and ha.s made a state- ment before Major Turner, of the Intelligence Department, at Dongola. This man denies the treachery of Fang Pacha, who was his fellow officer. He says that 20 days before the capture of the city Gordon urged all civilians incapable of bearing arms to leave, in order to av id starvation, and sent a letter to the Mandi, worded: Behold these people now that I have had them six months. Do yon, therefore, act likewise. Feed, support them. Even as I hive done up 'o the present date, (Li von in Abdullah gives (be number of persons left in Khirtoum before it was *aken as about 14,000, includieg the military. Fang Pacha, he chclares, was kilted because he had served the ,nfidel. He believes that four or five thousand civilians and soldiers were massacred, though several grappled with heir murderers and strangled many in their despair. Gor- ton, together with a European doctor,' an interpreter, and two other Men, killed 200 Araks at least from tne Palace,

I and when their ammunition WAS exhausted the eastern door was thrown open, and Gordon, ," Calm And serene,' smoking na cigarette, and carrying a sword in his right hand, appeared. There WAR a pause for a moment, but one near him raised a rifle and shot the General dead. speak the truth,' added AbdulLah, 'and lie not, Allah knows.' The dervishes then asseMbled and killed the survivors. Councillor BROADBENT said that Alderman Webster's inviry implied a c3rtain danger of soma nuisance arising from the manure which must necessarily came from the stables. He did not know of any such nuisance, bat he mentioned that there was a kind of beddinVor litter used that had the advantae of eying off no smell—he alluded to what was called moss-litter.

div.head: SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION IN WARRINGTON.

The School Attendance Committee reported that the aver- age attendance at the dlferent schools daring the month of May was 6,927, and for the corresponding period last year 6,776; increase 171. Alderman WEBSTER moved, and Councillor Limos seconded, the adoption of these minutes. Couocillor BRO&DBENT asked whether it waa part of the duties of that committee to see that the accommodation at the various schools was sufficient, or whether that duty was left to the Government inspector and the managers of the dift,rent schools. Alderman WEBSTER thought that was left to the Govern- ment inspector and managers. Councillor BooArmENT asked the Town Clerk as to the duties of School Attendance Committees.
The TOWN CLERK said he was not prepared to define the duties of a School Attendance Cammittee.

Councillor BROADBENT hoped the committee had the powers he alluded to. lie bel eyed the accommodation was deficient at many of the schools, and with regard to one he knew that the Government inspector had stid that tin., lees the accommodation was increased be would have to take some strenuous measures to sea that it was provided. He (Mr". Broadbent) did not know whether that accommo- dation had been provided, but he rather thought it bad not. He thought that in many of the schools of the town the accommodation and appliances were behind the time. He would not say a word that was disrespectful about masters as he thought they were of a seperior kind and very well qualified for their duties, but the teaching appliances of many if not most of the schools in Warrington were insuf- ficient and behind these times, when not only ban the edu- cation been improved, but what was quite as important, the supply of fresh air, the ventilation, the arrangement of the children generally, and drill, which was found to be of very great advantage to children. If the School Attendance Com- mittee had the power he should be very glad to see them exercise a greater power of supervision over the schools in Warrington than they had hitherto done, because he thought it was very much required.

Councillor JOLLEY Said t:louncillor Broadbent was en- tirely under a misapprehension. As a school manager he could tell Councillor BroAdhent that toe schools were amply sufficient, and the two schools he WAS connected with were spending large sums of money imoroving them in ventila- tion and that sort of thing. The accommodation according to the number of people in the town WAS sufficient for this year and the next year, and perhaps for some years to come. _

Alderman CitaNDLEY did not agree with Councillor Broadbent that the School Attendance Committee should have more p3wers. He thought it would saddle a corporate body with immense responsibility if they went in for the management of schools. Councillor Sorrow said that question was very fully dis- cussed on a recent Occasion whoa they went into the ques- tion of having a School Board in the town. and then they came to the conclusion that a Schol Bowd was un- necessary, and that they had ample accommodation in the schools at present existing. The MAYOR thougqt there were a certain class of schools where the quantity of air and other sanitary accommoda- tion were not of the best kind, and if some mode of supervi- sion could be taken some good might come out of it. But so far as Warrington was c mcerned be thought they might congratulate themselves upon the excellency, not only of their schools, but all° upon the accommodation which they at present enjoyed. Alderman VirmasYnn said there were new schools that had been erected or were b drag erected, and he thought these new schools would compare in any respect with those of I any other town in the excellency of their arrangements and I I; facilities. He was of opinion that the School Attendance Committee might have more powe-s which he , thought would be as well exercised by a Town Council as by a School Board. There were ;no doubt certain portions of the town where mere school accommodation was wanted. A school was wanted lat Bewsey, for instance, and there were some other places besides where they would be usaful. He also referred to the fact that some schools refused to take in half timers. 1 The minutes were then passed. I PARK AND BATHS COM3IITTEE IN THE PARK.

SATURDAY, JULY 11, 1885. 14. , Leaders of the new Government have to ,4en, and we now know what they intend 0, and to leave undone, during the few vilth that they s will be in office prior to the b,rteral Election. They know that they ~St on sufferance—that they hold power tk°V the grace of Mr. GuinszoNE ;" and are going to take things as easy as they a',u) and wind up the business of Parliament 170!oon as possible. This latter considera- for4 is at any rate something to be thankful ; the shorter the pertod.of time the Tories in office the less mischief they are prtY to do. According to their statements 41z;ren in Opposition everything at home and -oad that the GLADsToNE Government there doing was ruinously wrong ; but now Qthey have come into power they are lif,l4lg up the threads just as they have been ow. down. ' . It must do t be that they have dis- 4red that the skein is not tangled, or, if it lk A‘uat they are unable to unravel it. Lord 110oLpa CHURCHILL said it was "terrible Nvs:: when Mr. GLADsToNE announced in Pit Rouse of Commons that there was .a or-,ll3ect of a peaceful settlement with Russia Lo`"e Afghan boundary dispute; but to day is SALISBURY is Premier, and, although otltt'l this matter walking in the track marked NI h his predecessors—terrible as it may e 443;4)rd Ris.NDOLPH has not only nothing to v4„4gainst it, but becomes a party to the 41cfr Policy he had previously condemned. re; ed his lordship, and the red of the 4110 in the House of Commons, have tor te.h'llY foLnd that they have a great regard ot Ib'e Opinion of Mr. GLADSTONE. It is :11ter-arlY weeks since they assailed him with itiro-,ruPtions and were ill-mannered towards tha the point of brutality; but such is the 4ge that has come over them that, on Tevening, Lord R. CHURCHILL, as It' evening, was constrained to "thank "tte,ht hon gentleman for his considerate 4441:1.4:aguanimou5 treatment." We have no ZervaT this sudden conversion of the Con- it shows a lack of honesty, and is fear. It would seem that- -ereif thPr"ider • fashioned them hollow, 151 Mer • „Ate la, they might their principles swallow. I,Cory 4119ther instance. It was part of the rlktlibl),°licY when in opposition to attack the —E) and Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL :0 far on one occasion as to describe perhaps the very worst ruler whom "le centres of Oriental abominations ilserml?roduce ' he was "one of the most `ll, "‘"tab' th /Ptia le wretches who ever occupied the thtoWi • throne " It was thought by thus n , It g Plenty of mud upon the KHEDIVE G qv rne of it would stick to the Liberal /VA ernill 111)-1tai .TEwFix, of whom all this I„„ the ,„ It must be remembered, put s, Lorone by England and France when Atisl'ultv was Foreign Minister, and

yet he could remain silent whilst the KHEDIVE was being vilified by a henchman. But it may be said that it is since that Lord SALIS BURY has found TEwFix to be a double dyed traitor. Nothing of the kind; this is what his lordship, by way, we presume, of apology, felt it necessary to say of him on Monday evening in the House of Lords :—" Among the many difficulties with which we have had to deal in Egypt, we have had one compensa- tion. We have had to deal with a KHEDIVE who has throughout the whole of this calamit- ous history shown himself loyal and steadfast to England, and to whom therefore we are bound by every consideration of honour" What a pity it is that some "consideration of honour" did not prompt Lord SALISBURY to say a good word for the KHEDIVE when Lord R. CHURCHILL sought to kick him whilst he was down! And what are we to think of the new Cabinet which includes two politi- cians so diametrically opposed to each other—the ore holding that TEWFIK should be deposed and ARABI PASHA recalled; the other that we are bound to TEWFIK by every consideration of honour? Lord SALISBURY'S Ministry betray the same disregard of consistency and of principle in deciding to attempt the government of Ire- land without renewing the Crimes Act, or any portion of the Crimes Act. It will still be fresh in mind that when the Liberals came into office in 1880 they were roundly abused by the Tories because of their deter- mination to rule Ireland, if possible, without coercion. The humane policy of the Liberals failed ; and Lord SALISBURY was for a time incessant in his denunciation of the folly of Mr. GLADSTONE for not laying a heavier hand upon Ireland. Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL .took up the cue, and "bet- tered the instruction." Notwithstanding the repressive measure which was ultimately passed to put down the Land League, the fire-eating member for Woodstock was not satisfied. He wanted more coercion, and this is how, some eighteen months ago, he reviled the Government :—" This is the school," he said, "which bargains for Par- liamentary support with the assassins of ; Phoenix Park; this is the scho‘.l which, in order to defeat the Tory party, will join hands again with Mr. PARNELL in his demand for ' the independance of Ireland." We will not retort upon Lord RANDOLPH that he and his friends have done a good deal of bargaining of late with "the assassins," as we do not think Mr. PARNELT, and his friends havedonct I anything:to warrant so opprobrious a desig- nation. But we are fully entitled to point the moral and adorn the tale; for his lordship in the same speech goes on to say—" The Tory party is not prepared to give an inch to the Irish party in this matter. It is resolved . to stand firm, and," he adds, " I tell Vou sincerely that on this question the Tory party is entitled to your support." Sincerely How does this look now in face of the fact that Lord CHURCHILL and Lord SALISBURY are members of a Government which, in order to save its political soul,--a soul, after all, not worth saving---has entered into an alliance with the Parnellites, the result of which is that there is to be no coercive act of any kind ? We are not defending coercion; we believe with Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. that it is a hateful incident; but we are justified in pointing to the spectacle of the Tory party debasing itself on this question—grovelling in the mud---naked and not ashamed. The reign of "hollowness, and cant, and lies," has commenced ; but it will not be for long; it will end, let us hope, before the year is at an end.

Mr. BRADLAUGH, as was to be expected of him, presented himself at the table of the House of Commons, on Monday, on the re- assembling of Parliament. The order exclud- ing him from the precincts of the House having as a Sessional Order expired, it was due to his constituents that he should again put in an appearance as their representative. It should never be forgotten in this contro- versy that the issue is one that is wider than the personality of the member for Northamp- ton. It may or may not be a small matter whether a particular individual is boycotted ; but there can be no question as to the prin ciple at stake when the House of Commons takes upon itself to say that it will not re ceive the elect of a constituency against whose title to sit no legal objection can be taken. Such conduct—and it is the conduct of the House of Commons so far in dealing with Mr. BRADLAUGH—is, as Mr. GLADSTONE has again and again said, unconstitutional 'and illegal; and if constituencies were as jealous as they should be of their hoont o osurloanngd their rights, Northampton would n have been left with an unsatisfied claim to re- presentation. It is gratifying to see that, as far as he has been able, Mr. BRADLAUGH has done his duty by Northampton, and that Northampton, in electing him four times, has done its duty by him. They have but to con- tinue fighting the battle together; they must win in the end. To those who would find fault with the course taken by Mr. BRADLAUGH in hislong struggle with Parliament, we would say that he has throughout done better by the House of Commons than the House has done by him. He might, had he thought fit, have presented himself on Monday without a word of warning, but he gave due notice of his intention to approach the table or the House with a view to taking the oath and his seat. He owes no mercy to the members of the new Government • but he was consi- derate even of them. He could have walked up to the SPEAKER while, for instance, Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH was awaiting the opportunity to present himself after re-elec- tion, and thus have thrown the Tory camp into confusion, seeing that the new leader of the House would not, in that case, have been in his place to introduce the resolution which he afterwards moved. But he fore- bore; he waited patiently, and it is some satisfaction to know that, although the reso- lution against him was again carried, it was carried by a reduced majority, notwithstand- ing that there had been no special " whip " on the part of the Liberals. Mr. BRADLATIGIT has behaved well; he is doing the right thing in the right way, and his triumph is not far distant.

The Town Council of Warrington was oc- cupied fora considerable time on Tuesday in discussing what Councillor SUTTON not in- aptly called "a sore point," namely, the pro- vision made in the Market for itinerant drapers, &c., to the disadvantage of shop- keepers. There can be no question that the primary object of a market is to provide a place for the sale of vegetable produce, and, if it could be shown that the Markets Com- mittee were neglecting the purveyors of this class of goods in order to accommodate itin- erant vendors of other goods, there would be a good ground for complaint. But, judging horn the report of the proceedings of the Council, this does not appear to be the case Nor does it seem that the drapers, &c., are

f specially favoured as to terms. Alderman CH kNDLEY, as chairman of the Markets Com- mittee, states that "they charged them to the fullest extent per yard the Act allowed." What more can the Committee do? There is astory told of a lawyer who was brought to book by his legal brethren for accepting less than the prescribed fee. He admitted that he had done wrong, very wrong, but, he pleaded, it was due to himself to say be had taken all he could get—he had taken every penny that his client had. The Markets Committee have a better defence even than the man of law ; they not only take all they can get, but all they e entitled to get. It is beside the mark to ' talk of charging the drapers "something in addition to the rent they paid to go towards the rates of the borough.' Rent in this in- stance includes rates, and the ratepayers profit by the transaction precisely to the extent of the profits on the Market. The remedy is to be sought, as Aldetman WEBSTER suggested, in an Act of Parliament to enable the Committee to charge higher rates. Exclusion of any section of "market folk" in order to improve the trade of the shopkeepers is out of the question. It would be an interference with the freedom of trade which would be unwarranted, and one which no community could enforce with- out, in the long run, suffering from it. Old i'rotection is dead, and we do not think he will be resurrected in Warrington. It should be borne in mind, too, that market drapers have their use in relieving the ordinary shop- keeper of stock which is soiled, and damaged, ; and out of fashion. Damaged goods have to !be sold, and they have to be sold at a ; damaged price. It is a convenience to the shopkeeper to be rid of them ; it is a conve- nience to the itinerant draper to take them : off his hands; and it is a convenience to those who cannot pay a first-class price for first-class articles to do the best they can with their money. It is a question of supply and demand, and to interfere with it would be mischievous. By all means let there be "ample room and verge enough "for the supply of poultry and other choice things 'for the Alderman or Justice "with fair round belly with good capon lined ;" but at the same time let us show some regard for the .le In Operative, who, in the struggle to make both ends meet, would go to the Market for cheap drapery for his small ' wife and large faindy. We must keep to sound principles—free trade, a fair field, and no favour.

I rr, r , HE tABERAL CANDIDATE FOR THE WIDNES DIVISION.— The lelyeal Council of the Widnes division have unani- mously chosen Mr. E. B. Mnepratt, J.P , chemical manu- facturer, to contest the conetituency at the general election. The Council or "400" is divided into the Widnes, Gar- ston, Much Woolton, and Huyton sections, and during the present week meetines have been held at each of these p'ace+. The suggestion of the Executive Council that Mr. Muepratt should be the Liberal candidate has been received with gratification and adopted by each section without a , dissentient voice being raised. The formal resolution r passed reads as follows :--e• That this meeting adopts Mr. lE. K. Musprett as the Liberal candidate for the represen- tation in Parliament for the Widnes division of South- Weep Lancashire, and pledges itself to use all lawful means t secure his return," We are indebted tic Mr. H. B. Shores, ; the general secretary of the Widnes divieion, for this infor- , metier). Mr. Muspratt is president of the Widnes Liberal As- sociation, and has always taken a prominent part in political ! matters in the county. His views ere of the advanced type, , and he is gifted with the power of placing them before an audience in a flueut and clear manner. He enjoys the thorough confidence of the Liberal party in the division, and a stronger or more suitable candidate could not easily have been found. • MARRIAGE AT HALTON. OR Wedneshay morning at Halton Perish Church, Mr. Frank H. Tate, brother of Mr Norman Tate, of Liverpool, was married to Miss Agnes Pierpoint, youngest daughter of Mr. Robert Pierpoint. tan.. nor, Halton-road, Beacom. Mr. Tate who is a ebemist at Messrs. Blythe and Co's. works, Church, near Accrington. temente: occupied a responsible position at the Camden Soap Works, Runcorn. Both bride and bridegroom are well known in the neighhourhood, and the ceremony was wit- nessed by a large cengregetion of friends and acquaintances. The bride was attired in a dress of cream cashmere and coin, trimmed with lace, and her brow was wreathed with etephenatis and orange blossom, from which depended a long veil. The bridesmaids were Miss Pierpeint, sister of the bride ; MlS`i Tate and Miss Mona Tate, nieces of the bridegroom. Their attire consisted of biscuit-coloured muslin dreerfes with crimson velvet trimming, and lace hats. while each carried a basket of roses in her hand. Mr. T. Irwin, of Accrington, was the best man. The wedding party included Mr. Red Mrs Pierpoint, Alderman and Mrs. B intock (Wolverhampton), Alderman and Mrs Dickinson (Wolverhampton), Mr. William Bantock (Manchester), Dr. and Mrs Granville Bantoek (London), Miss Littler (Run- corn), Mr. Bantock Pierpoint (London), Mr. and Mrs Nor- man Tate (Oxton), Miss Amy Tate (Wells), Mr- W. J. Tate (London), Mr. Fred Pierpoint (Warrington), Mr. R. W. Pierpoint, Mr. T. B. Pierpoint, and Mr. A. E. Pierpoint. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. J. Lockwood, vicar. The presents were very numerous and costly. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD.—The annual meeting was held at the cemetery on Wednesday. Presentee-Messrs. Moss, Coleburn, Littler, Rogerson, and Salkeld (secretary).—Mr. Colehurn moved in eulogistic term that the beet thanks of the Board be accorded to Mr. James Elandley, J.P., for the able manner in which he had occupied the ch fir during the pest twelve mouths—Mr. Rogerson seconded the proposi- tion, which was unanimously carried.—Mr. Moss proposed that Mr. William Littler be appointed chairman for the ensuing veer. Mr. Littler hid always taken an active in- terest in the business of the Board, and his services had been of the ereetest advantage to the ratepayers. Mr. Moss was sure that if appointed, Mr. Lit,ler would be a credit to the Board.—Mr. Coleburn seconded the motion' and it was agreed to unanimously—Mr. Littler thanked the Board for the honour they had conferred upon him. lie should have preferred that some one else bail been appointed to the posi- tion. hut he would endeavour with the assistance of the members te carry out the duties to the satisfaction of the Board and the ratepavers.—On the proposition of Mr. Roger- son, seconded by Mr. Moss, Mr. William Mellor was up- pointed vice-chairman. The Fume,' Committee was con- stituted as follows :—Meesrs. Mess. Handley, Norman, and B. Imison.—lt was renerted that rfuring the tbree months ended the 25th Jane there were 102 interments, an increase of le unen the corresponding period last year The fees received during the same period amounted to £96 13s 6d, an increase of £8 is 7d. The report of the Finance Com- mittee, adopted on tbe motion of Mr. Moss, seconded by Mr. coleburn, stated that the receipts for the past month were £29 4s, of which £l2 2s had been paid in wages, and the balance, £l7 2+, deposited in the bank. Accounts amount- ing to £23 4s 4a were passed for payment. DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.—A meeting of this Board was held in the Boardroom, DaresburY, on Thursday afternoon, the Chairman, Mr. E. Green- all, presiding.—The Chairman said that as he was absent from the previous meeting, when he was re-elected, he would take that opportunity of thank- ingthem, and he expressed the hope that their business would be as pleasantly gone through this year as in past years.—The Clerk read the auditor's report, from which it appeared that the accounts were found correct by him.—The Chairman : That is satisfactory; has he surcharged anybody? (Laughter.)—The Clerk: No, sir.—The matter of the allege,l obstruction to the highway caused by Mr. J. Smith, at Stretton Hall, was brought before the Board by the Chairman, and after some conver- sation a committee consisting of Messrs. Knowles, Whitley, and Barber was appointed to meet Mr. Smith and endeavour to have the obstruction re- moved. Unless this was done, the Chairman said, it would be necessary for the Board to proceed by indictment, as an action would lie against theToard were an accident to occur through the obstruction. —This was all the business.
