The evidence showed that the drceased, who was 53 years of age. bad suffered front bronchitis and heart disease for several years, and on the morning of his death was delirious. He was in bed when his fellow lodger went to work at twenty minutes to seven. At seven o'clock be entered the Swag lan and had a glass of whiskey mixed with coffee. When leaving he fell down against the wall and was brought into the house and the doctor sent for, but he died before his arrival.—The jury returned s verdict to the effect that death probably resulted from natural causes.

ing. On-the first hearing of the case against Gehon, it will be remembered it was alleged that a large quantity of liquor had been supplied to him and other members of the corps by the officers in com- mand, at Warrington, at the conclusion of the an- nual training which recently took place at Altcar. In order that some inquiry might be made into the statement, the hearing of the case was adjourned until Monday. On being called, however, the de- fendent did not appear.—ln reply to the Bench, Major and Adjutant Ritche, who was present in the court, denied that any offence of the nature alleged to have been committed had occurred on the regi- ment leaving Altcar. The canteen had closed at half-past nine o'clock, and was not open to militia- men at Warrington. The statement made by Gehon, as to Colonel O'Malley supplying drink was absolu- tely without foundation.—Mr. Aspinall said that it was satisfactory that the allegation had been so completely denied. THE NEW ARCHDEACON OF BLACEBURN.—We understand that the Bishop of Manchester has con- ferred the archdeaconry of Blackburn, void by the resignation of Archdeacon Edward Birch, upon the Rev. Robert Atherton Rawstorne, M.A., vicar of St. Leonard's, Balderston, and Proctor in Convocation. The new Archdeacon is the descendant of a Lanca- shire family for many centuries settled at Lum and Hutton, not a few of his ancestors having served the office of high sheriff. One, Captain Edward Rosthorne, of Newall, was one of the six captains who bravely assisted the Countess of Derby during the siege of Lathom House in 1643. The Arch- deacon's father was the Rev. R. A. Rawstone, M.A., irector of Warrington for 24 years, and subsequently rector of South Thoresby, Lincolnshire, and after- wards vicar of Penwortham, Preston. He was edu- cated at Rugby by the late Dr. J. Prince Lee (then assistant master to Dr. Arnold), and graduated at Brazenose College, Oxford (of which he was Hul- meian Exhibitioner), in 1846; ordained by the late Bishop of Manchester, in 1848 he became curate to his father at Penwortham, whom he succeeded as incumbent in 18.52. Subsequently (in 1859) he was appointed to the benefice of Balderston. The mew Archdeacon, who holds moderate Church views, is exceedingly popular in the archdeaconry, as was evidenced by his election in 1880 as Proctor in Con- vocation. ' MRS. S. A. Sin RICHARD CROSS.—Speaking on Wednesday night at a dinner given by the Lord Mayor to the Archbishop of Canterbury and the Bishops, Sir Richard Cross said that apart from politics the people of the country would insist upon having one thing, and that was a Government that knew its own mind and stuck to it. England must know that she was strong, and the world must know it too. She must, however, not only know how to use her strength, but how not to use it, unless its exercise was called for by good and honest reasons. The Government whose policy was firm would, he believed, command the confidence of the country, whether the constituencies were large or small.— I Sir Richard has consented to receive a deputation ' on Tuesday next from the Central Emigration Society, in favour of the aSsisted emigration of chil- dren from indlistrial schools and orphanages. Mr. Rankin, M.P., will introduce the deputation. , A PLEA FOR DIRECT TMTION.—The following circular has been issued by. the St: HelenA Liberal Association :—" Working-men and the Income-tax. It is being industriously circulated in St. Helens that Colonel Gamble, the adopted candidate of the local Liberal Association, is in favour of income-tax being paid by every mau earning Li a week and upwards. Colonel Gamble is not in favour of such a tax unless all other taxes be abolishe-1, when, instead , of every glass of beer or spirits which a man drinks, every cup of tea or coffee made in his home, and every pipe of tobacco which he smokes, being made an indirect Medium for heavy taxation, all these, with every subject of taxation would be free; and the poor and rich alike would then only pay for Government in exact proportion to their actual income. It has been proved over and over again that this would relieve the working classes, who at ' present bear more than their share of the burdens of the State, from the payment of thousands upon thousands a year; and, in addition, every man, under such an arrangement, would know exactly what taxation he was paying, and want to know More urgently than be does now, where it was it,ll going."

The monthly meeting of this Board was bald on Thurs- day. Mr. T. S. Timmis, J.P. presiding. Present—Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. J. Brock, IP., H. W. Deacon, J. B. Intim, J. (!o 3, U. Davis,, G. H. Danby (clerk).
A CE-17909 OF SCHOOL CHILDEODT.‘

The District Education Committee teported that during the holidays the attendance officers were employed in tak- ing a census of the children of the district, the results being presented in a tabular ferrn.—Mr. Deacon, in moving the adoption of the report, dealt with the tables. The number of houses in Widnes, he said, was 5,097, against 5,092 last year. Tue numbw of empty' houses had decreased from 564 last year to 387. The houses in course of con- struction were 12, against 4 last year, and they were all in the West district. Tne scnoal accommodation at St. Bede's had been increased from 305 to 765, and at St. Mary's from 706 to 806. The total accommodation at the schools was 6397, against 5.835 last year, a very considerable increase. The number of children between 3 and 13 years of age had increased from 6,665 10 6,914 this year, but this was note° great an advance as in previous years. The number of children receiving instruction at private schools had in- creased from 166 to 203, and there were 1,275 children at- tending no school, against 1,187 last year. The number of children between 3 and 5 years had, however, increased from 1,372 oo 1467, so that these increa,es balanced each other. The number of children who ought to be on the rolls was 5,760, against 5,636 last year, and the number of children who were on the rolls was 5,637, against 5,486 last year. There were, therefore, 123 children not on the rolls, against 150 last rear. This had been a gradual reduction in the number not on the rolls, but although theoretically there ought not to be any, there would always be from 100 to 150. The children between 3 and 5 years of age on the rolls numbered 367, and the number of children on the rolls between 13 and 14 years of age was 201. Estimating the populatioa of the town at 30,000, the proportion of school- goidg children to the population was 1 to s•9s,—The Chair- man considered these figures very satisfactory, and the re- port was adopted.

MR. BRUNNER'S CANTAW.I'TU.RE.—MEETING AT WESTON. On Tuesday evening Mr. J. T. Brunner, the Liberal can. didate for the Northwich divjion, addrebsed a meeting or working-min at Weston. Being unable to obtain the use of any building, the gathering took place in the open air on a piece of ground overlooking the quarry of Messrs. Handley, and although the weather was very cold, and threatening clouds hung overhead, upwards of 200 persons were present. Mr. Thomas Handley presided, and he was supported on the platform, which had been erected, by the candidate, Messrs. James Handley. J.P., S. C. Beckett, J. Midwood, B. Kniveton, James Bill, W. Handley. O. Leak, and several working-men from the village. Previous to the commencement of the proceedings Mr. Brunner, accom- panied by the gentlemen named, walked through the vil- lage, and op their return the Wesleyan Brass Band took up a position behind them and played "The Pilot of the State" in good style. The Chairman in a few appropriate words introduced

Mr. Branner,whose remarks were listened to with intel- ligent interest. He asked those present on which side they would range themselves. On the side of the men who since 1867 had been trying to get votes for them and had at last succeeded, or on the side of the men who up to twelve months ago firmly and deliberately resisted the granting of votes to grown up men like those he saw before him. Many. years ago he made up hie mind that he should be on the ' side of proeress and liberty, on that side which was united in endeavouring to promote the comfort and well-being of all. and to bring about peace, honour, and goodwill amongst men. Theetiberal party, especially those who were not too proud to, call themselves -Itadicele—(hear, hear)—con- siderea that the honour of England was just as much pledged to weat he had been describing, just as much pledged to secure their interests and his, as it was pledged to find a good front:er for Afghanistan- (Applause.) The Tories were very' fond of claiming all the credit for the defence and honour of England. He did not give way to that. He de- clared that he maintained the honour of Engteed as much as any man opposed to him, but he did not talk very much about Egypt and Afghanistan and the Cameroone. (Laugh- ter and applause.) To his mind the honour of England was dimmed as long as there was one pauper out of 36 of the population—as long as every 36 men all the year round had to maintain a pauper. This he c nesidered to be a shame to our Goverament. Alluding to taxation, Mr. Brunner quoted Adam Smith to the effect that taxes were the payment for servicea rendered to the indivhtual by that combination of the individual that was called the State; that every man ought to pay in just proportion to his in- come, and that nobody shoced escape. By an illustrative he argued that the Squire with ten times the incerne of the farmer paid the poor rate as a rule upon only a tenth of his income, the farmer paid upon his Oct profits. Was there any sense or injustice in tbie ? In imperial taxes the work- ing-man spend more upon taxed articles in proportion to the total amount that came into the house every wok than did the rich men. The poor men paid enough and too mach in proportion to their means. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) The Right Hon. Joseph Chatiberlein, who was a very good friend to working-men, made a statement not long ago to the effect that rich men paid in the total taxa- tion of the country 3 per cent, of his income, arid that the average working-men paid 6 or 7 per cent. None of them knew really what Gov- ernment cost the country: but he was thoroughly satisfied that if it were known how much locil and imperial governe ment did cost, that the people would pretty wen make it cast lees and get better value for their money. (Hear, hear.) Alluding to international trade. Mr. Brunner ridi- culed the notion held by men who could see no farther than their noses, that because the impo-ta were 50 or 60 milliqns of pounds above the exports th t the country was getting poorer, and explained that Etegleud had nine tenths of the carrying trade of the world, and was really the re- epient of the 50 millions. Now there was a gentleman living not far away who before many weeks were over would talk to them a lot of arrant nonsense about the ques- tion of foreign trade. He was very fond of saying that they must make the foreigner pay. And the way in which he would elo this was to put a tax upon what was broeght into the country; he would not let foreign corn come into Eng- land without patting a tax upon it. And this was what was called making the foreigner pay. He (Mr. Brunner) would smash that notion utterly. (Hear, hear.) Salt was sent to India, which when it left the Weever was worth 5s or C 3 per ton. When it arrived it India a duty of £5 101 was placed upon it. Who paid that duty—tee foreigners, who in this case were the English or the people of India. Was it not clear that the people of India paid it. Yet there were men to all appearances sane who would inei.t upon it that by putting an import duty upon goods we made the foreigner pry. To his mind it was only an idea fit for Bedfam. God had given varied gifts to each section of the earth's surface, and He intended that those gifts should be freely exchanged from one nation to the other the wide world over. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Mr. James elendley, J.P., moved a reeolation expressing approval of Mr. Brunner's candidature in a neat speech, and it was seconded by Mr. James Ball. Mr. B. Kniveton supported the motion ire a spirited and eloquent speech which frequently elicited applause, referr- ing to the numerous great measures passed by the Liberals to increase the happiness and well-being of the people, and to the fact that they bad always been opposed by the Tories.
The resolution was passed unanimously, and Mr. Brunner in replying moved a vote of thanks to the ctairma:-.., which was accorded by acclamation.
MEETCNCI AT _HALTON LAST NIGHT.

Last night another of the series of ward meetings _ar- ranged by the Runcorn Liberal Association was lfeed at the old Court-room, Halton, under the presidency of Mr. J. N. LeHo. There was a good attendance, and Mr. J. 'l'. Brunner, the candidate, and Mr. Joseph Forster, the secretary to the People's League, were present. The Chair nan, in introducing Mr. Branner, gave his reasons for holding Liberal principles, observing that the Liberal party had been the only true friends of the people. (Applause.) He was interrupted by several Tories in the room during the course of his speech. Mr. Brunner, who was cordially received, said he wel- corned opposition. The Liberal pirty was the party 0! freedom and free discussion—(hear, bear)—and never so long as he was with them would he be a p ate, to putting it down. Mr. Lello had asked a gentleman (Mr. Acton) to answer a plain question, and, as had not infrequently hap- pened before, he was not able to. (L tughter.) This gen- tleman, who had been a Conservative for a good many years, and who beliewd that a Conservative party wouid have given the people votes, was a neighbour of theirs. (Hear, bear.) Could any one of them tell of a single occasion on which this gentleman had exerted himself to fget them votes? (Cries of "No.") Could they tell when any Conservative speaker came to Halton to advocate them getting votes? (" No.") Speaking of the achittvements of the Liberal party, Mr. Brunner said it wte the work of the L•betals that bread was cheap in the mouths of the people, that food of all kinds was plentiful, and that men could get money to buy fo id with. (A Voice : Thett,'s very little money stirring—Mr. W. Wright : He's one that wont work when he has the chance, air. Load laughter and applause.) Kories did not Hee to work, and the leaders of the Tory party lived upon those wno did work. (Applause.) The landlolds had robbed •the peovle of mildons and millions of pounds, and they. WriL doing it to-day. (Hear, hear.) The night before not a meting i was h. Id in a township not far away in this division, and t was a very interesting meeting. Mr. Verdin, his opposent, was present—(applause) —and Mr. Barns took the chair, and said that he did not approve of him (Mr: Blazoner) because he had declined to. support Sunday cio.ong. This was not strictly accurate. He had said that if a majority of the people of a neigh- bourhood wished to have public-houses closvel on Sunday, let thorn say so, and he was wilting that they should be closed. He was sorry Ile W. El. Verdin said that Mr. Hob,rt Veidin—and he had no doubt he spoke with full outhority on the emestlon—would never vote for him. Did they remember that Mr. R. Verdin submitted his claims to the decision of the Liberal party? if he did not intend to remain a Liberal, why didn't he say so ? (Applause.) In another part of his speech he told them that his "big brother" would he a better represeetative than himself. That " big brother "—(laughter)—was a oirector of the company, and if they obj,cted to their works going on Sunday, did not they think it would be more manly oft his part to come to the directors' meeting and seer HO Instead of endeavouring to make political capital out of it. (Applause.). Speaking of Mr. W. H. Verdiner effort on behalf of cyclists, Mr. Brunner said Mr. Verdin had been trying to find out how long twilight lasted With a proud and digni- fied air, Mr. Verdin informed the magistrates that he had written to the Astronomer Royal to find out Low long twilight lasted—(langhter)—and the Astronomer Royal had told him to look at Whittaker's Almanackice(ReintzetWhaedt. laughter.) Mr. Verdin could not see any He did not know that the Astronomer Royal was poking fun at him. Mr. Verdin's proposition would have been laughed out of court if he had not quietly suggested to Mr. Horatio Lloyd that the cyclists might have z(bAooioanuosem.)ton on Liberal evenings, and it was so settled. pp A resolution to support Mr. Brunner at the poll was carried enthusiastically.

Thomson, civil engineer and professor of natural HALL, WARRINGTON. philosophy at Glasgow University, who was next called, gave evidence that if the upper estuary were silted up the The improvements to the Public Hall which were scour upon the bar would cease and Liverpool bar would be blocked.—The Chairman : If 'there were no Mersey there projected some time ago by the directors, and sane- w tioned by the shareholders, are being rapidly pushed would be no Liverpool ?—Witness: No. The taking away forward. The object of the alterations is to provide of the :and waters from the estuary would probably be dis- more ample stage space, and better private accemnao- estrous to Liverpool, and the formation of a training wall dation for the companies who from time to time per- along the Cheshire shore would probably be disastrous to form at the Hall. The want of these facilities has at Liverpool. times been very keenly felt, and some actors, who, like musicians, have the reputation of being a some- what irritable race, have protested that ' they would not again appear at the Hell if they were not more suitably provided for. The ,directors, apart from other oonsiderations, could not ignore complaints of this sort, and consequently wisely, decided to do their utmost to increase the populariey of the Halt, and for this purpose have undertaken the present alterations, which are estimated to cost something like £ t,OOO. So far as accommodation goes the result of the improve- ments will be to slightly lessen the capacity of the gallery, but this, so far at all events as political meetings are concerned, will be . counter• acted by the fact the; larger numbers will be able to share in the honours of the plat- form. The designing and superintendence of the alterations have been entrusted to Mr. Alfred Derby- shire, F.1.8.A., a well-known theatrical architect. The more noticeable changes that will be or have been made may be briefly mentioned. In place of the old platform a permanent stage will be erected, and will be provided with all the necessary facilities for the satisfactory production of dramatic pieces. The corn- fort of the performers has been carefully considered, and on the " prompt " side of the stage are the dreea- ing rooms, and underneath the stage a small dressing room will also be made. EA,* of these will be fitted with appropriate conveniences, and there is to be a eeperate baggage entrance, the stage entrance thus being left clear for the artistes. The proscenium is flanked b.,* handsome pilasters terminating in foliating cepi- tale, the stage opthng being finished with a rich architrave in fibrous plaster. The eutrancee to the Hall will undergo some transformation, as the central entrance will run through what is at present the small hall, and this entrance will be flanked by lediee' and gentlem, n's retiring or cloak minis. ipareful atten- tion is given to the important matter of ventilation, prevision being male for a constant supply of fresh whileae exhanet in the shape of a powerful sun • burder will be placed in the centre of the ceiling. div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.

MONDAY. The case for the petitioners against the Manchester Ship Canal Bill was opened before the Select Committee at the 16th sitting on Monday morning. Mr. W. E. Forster pre- sided.—Speeches being reserved, Captain Graham Hills was at once called on behalf of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board; to whom he is the marine surveyor. Describing the tidal phenomena of the Mersey, he explained that at a 21ft. tide the water at Warrington was sft. higher than at the ha'-, and at Eastham. Hale Head, and Runcorn the tide was also pro rat 4 higher than at the bar. (At the request of the Chairman, iMr. Bidder, Q.C., promised to have these figures emboditid it, a table, Mr. Forster remarking that they bore very much on the allegation that the proposed channel would raise the water higher up the estuary.) The witness described the course of the three channels between the es- tuary and the sea, and stated that the head of the rock channel consisted of rock.—The Chairman: Then why don't the Liverpool people cat a channel through it ? The witness answered that they had a better one outside.—The Chairman: Supposing by Any mewl the tidal wave got further no the eeluary, would a greater volume of water enter the river ? Witness: I think not. It would appear that a very large addition to the upper estuary would brine in more water, but as a matter of fact the tide has turned and begun to run out at the bar by the time of high water at Liverpool. At high water at Warrington the tide has been ebbing nearly three hours at the bar. Witness calcula- ted that the promoters' works would involve an abstraction of tidal area at a 14ft. tide of 371 acres, representing 7,905,000 cubic yards of water, ;Lei of this eleven acres would be above Runcorn. He FTieved this abstraction would be materially prejudicial to the bar, while the inter- ruption of the land waters would be a serious detriment to

the upper estuary. The waters of the Weaver were also valuable to the estuary, and the proposed interference with those waters would constitute a dang.r.—The Chairman eh. served that the chart showed an encroachment of 240 acres in extent opposite Runcorn, and the contention on the part cf the opponents was the abstraction at or above Runcorn was more import,nt as regarded the effect on the bar than abstraction below that place. He wanted to know, therefore, for there must be some record, what was the state of the bar before that encroachment was made in 1873, and the state of the bar since that date.—A table was handed in showing the condition of the bar before and since 1873, and the Chairman read aloud the figures, which showed a consistent improvement in the depth of the bar since that date.—The witness observed that the encroachment resulted in the extension of the marshes in the estuary.—The Chair- man said all they bad to do with was the effect on the bar, and the bar seemed to have been worse in 1873 than • niece.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

Captain Graham Hills, marine surveyor of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, in further examination by Mr. Bidder, said that the high water marks in the upper estu Iry at present were nearly the same as they were in 1822,1 showing that the training effect of the lateral jails was compensated for in diminishing the sectional area of the channel.—The Chairman : It seems that no amount of scour or water in the outer estu sty flowing over the bar would have any scouring eff ,ct ? I have not said that it has not, for all the water having a velocity of half a mile an hour flowing over the bar would shift the sand ; but the effect on the bir is its proportion to what goes into the in- ner estuary.—The Chairman : I cannot reconcile these two statemetve—first, that so much of the water in the outer es- tuary as flows over the bar has an effect ; secondly, that it has no effect because that water does not go into the inner estuary ? No, it has no effect, because it does not in- crease the scouring power of the inner estuary —Witness was next examined as to accretions and erosions in the es- ' tuary.—The Chairman, referring to a table put in as to the capacity of the estuary and the depth of water on the bar, said it did not appear to him that those things had much to do with the bar. The year 1869 was a time when the reservoir was largest, and yet the two years about that period were the two worst years for the bar.—Mr. Bidder said that must not necessarily be assumed, because the ero- sion only began in 1869, and went over a good many years In further examination, witness said he had no participa- tion in the preparation of Mr. Lyster's plan. He did not agree with the plan, because it made no compensation for the abstraction of tidal water. WEDNESDAY.

Answering the Chairman, Captain Graham Hills, marine survsyor to the Mersey Dock Board, said he did not think the plan under consideration would do as much harm as that of last year. At any rate, the mischief would be very much longer in coming about. It was difficult to prophesy, but the general result of the present plan would be to pro- duce a permanent channel along the Cheshire shore The Chairman: I gather that you look with much more fear at this permanent channel than at the amount of abstraction ? Witness : It all works together in one direction.

Mr. G. F. Lyster, engineer to the Mersey Dock Board, was next called. Havihg detailed the nature and extent of the dock accommodation provided by the Board, the wit- ness said he had two grave objections to the promoters' plans. The first was that the works involved direct ab- straction from that part of the estuary where the mainte- nance of the entire estuarial capacity was of the utmost importance, and his second objection WAS that a permanent channel would be formed along the Cheshire shore. Silt- jog up would be caused in other parts of the estuary. This would prove dett imental to the normal c nrlition of the river, and would materially interfere with the channels that were now so important to the ports of Liverpool and Gars- ton. Of his two objections, the formation of a permanent channel was more important. The elongation of the deep opposite Etstham would draw waters from other parts of the estuary, and thus stereotype a channel to the exclusion of the channels now existing. In designing a plan as an alternative to that of last year, he endeavoured as much as possible to follow the natural configuration of the foreshore, and to minimise any intrusion upon it. The promoters had been guilty of serious plagiarism as regarded his plan. They bad simply mutilated his plan.—The Chairman asked the witness how be intended to carry out his plan without Interference with the estuary ? Witness answered that he proposed to keep close in shore, and not to touch upon estu- rial waters at all except at the ontlet.—Cross-examined by Mr. Michael, the witness said he put his plan before the Committee because it could safely be followed.—Then why object, to plagiarism ? Because yea have so materially altered what I consider to be the salient features of my plan that I cannot be responsible for it in any way.—The Chair- man: Your objection is not to plagiarism, but to the want of it. (Laughter )—The Chairman : Does your plan show upon it the works by which von give compensation ? Witness: No; it incidentally refers to where compensa- tion might be given—namely, in the Weaver.—ln answer to the Chairman, the witness stated that while attaching great weight to the question of abstraction he considered that the greatbst danger threatened by the prop ,ped works was the formation of the channel along the Cheshire shore.

div.head: THURSDAY.
div.p: THURSDAY.

In continuation, on Thursday, of the opponents' scien- tide evidence, Mr. Beacon, water engineor to the Liverpool Corporation, was called before the Select Committee. He was distinctly of opinion that the proposed works would cause a considerable rise in the sandbanks in the upper estuary and about the docks at the bar. They would operate as a training wall along the Cheshire shore; and the forma- tion of a channel along the shore would be ruinous to Liver- pool. Toe amount of obstruction would, he believed, be much larger than anything hitherto stated; and one result of this would be to cause a current in the lower channel.—

NOTES BY THE WAY.

The annual matchieiw;en the pick of the Gentlemen and Players has had an unsatisfactory termination. If, however, it bad gone on, there can be little doubt but that the Players would have scored a decisive victory. The Gentlemen had a good eleven, but it might have been con- siderably improved. _ _ .

The Lancashire and Essex Counties recommenced their matches last week, and it is to be hoped they may continue for a long time to come. The result was quite what every- one expected, and still the visiting eleven was not to be despised, as it included several good men. The Lancashire team, although not what was looked upon as a first rater, turned out to be, if the score is anything to go by, as good as most that have done duty so far this season. Sussex had to put up with a severe defeat at the hands of Surrey at the Oval. Surrey's total of 631 is the largest score in a first-class match this season. Towards this enormous total Mr. Roller ran ritt-,294, and Mr. W. Read had another big innings of 163. Against this Suss:x, although they played well, had no chance, and lost by an innings and 221 runs. In the match 1,041 runs were scored for the loss of 30 wickets. Derbyshire and Cheshire have played a draw, a very fitting termination to a match between them. Derbyshire, taken all round, did the best work; Wright, of Nantwich, with his twe inpings of 44 and 59 not out certainly saving the match for Cheshire.

Essex team took Derby on their journey southward, and cemmenced their match with Derbyshire. A very even day's c, icket was played en Monday, in which each side bad a completed innings, eight runs representing the advantage Derbyshire had over their opponents. In the second at- tempt Essex showed up wonderfully well, putting together 265, while their opponents only mustered 195, Essex thus winning by 62 runs. The Notts Committee bas been successful in its objec- tlons to Crossland and Brown, the former a Lancashire pro- fessi-nal and the latter a Cheshire professional. This action in respect to Crossland has put quite a different phase on the question of the Lancashire and Kent return match. There is, however, very little probability of this coming off unless the M.C.C. take some action in the matter. What they can do is hard to conceive now that the greatest stumbling block is removed. Of course, there still remains the question of Naeh's bowling, but the general opinion is that Lord Harris did not rely on this part of the case, and will, now that Crossland has been removed, not be averse to coming to terms. The position of the Lancashire Commit- tee is good, and they are determined to n,aintain their right to employ whatever bowlers they please so long as the judges as set up by the M.C.C. do not complain.

varnishes, Bco, which were valued at about £BO These were distributed about the premises. Witness had been on the premises ,that day, and had had pointed out to him sundry goods which he valued at about £22. In answer to Mr. Browne, witness said that he had taken the oath and it was binding on his conscience; otherwise he wonld not have taken it. He denied being an atheist. He had written letters to Spann threatening to expose him unless some money was given him. Mr. Browne ques- tioned witness closely as to various transactions. Wit- ness asked that his letters to the prisoner should be, referred to in the evidence, to show what his motive had been in writing them. One part he did not wish putting in the evidence, however, and that was a re- ference to his having taken theopinion of Mr. Brad- laugh!—Joshua Hewitt, a bailiff of the 'County Court, stated that he was put into possession of the pisoner's premises in Friars-green on the loth June. lie had since been making a search, and had found there a pair of new springs and a bench on one day, and on other days 14. pairs of shafts and bends, three pairs of new springs and a smithy.—Joseph Bridge, wheelwright, formerly in the employ of the prisoner, repeated evidence previously given by him.— By Mr.. Browne: Never said in the presence of Joseph and John Cross that it was a mere matter of money, and that he should go for who paid him best. Never said Mr. Garland had promised him £3, or that Mr. Garland would give him so many weeks wages. After hearing this evidence the magistrates sig- nified their intention of remanding prisoner, the hearing of the case having then occupied from ten o'clock in the morning until four o'clock in the after- noon.—Mr. Browne applied for bail, remarking that prisoner had a large family totally unprovided for.— Mr. Davies, while sympathising with prisoner's family, said that his instructions rendered it neces- sary for him to oppose bail.—Mr. Ridgway said that he should be satisfied with the same bail as the Beneh granted last week.—The magistrates said they would allow bail in the same amounts as last week, and remanded prisoner until Tuesday next. ADJOURNED BANKRUPTCY EXAMINA- TION. • An adjourned bankruptcy examination of Spann was fixed to be held at the Warrington County Court on Monday, before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. At the opening of the court there were present, be-n sides the Judge, the Registrar .(111r. Nicholson), and the Official Receiver (Mr. T. J. Ridgway.) The bank- rupt, Spann, was not present, and Mr. Ridgway ex- plained that he (Spann) was in custody, but it had been understood that if he wanted to appear there the chief constable would allow him to come. He (Mr. Ridgway) could only account for Span's non- appearance by supposing that he had not wisaed to appear.—Subsequently Mr. R. Davies, who is prose- cuting Spann on behalf of the Treasury, mentioned that criminal proceedings had been commenced which, he thought, might be preiudiced by the bank- rupt's being examined there that day. After some conversation his Honour adjourned the further hear- ing' of the bankrupt till the 13th August. L

RL MEETING AT WARRINGTON. SPEECHES OF MR. McMINNIES, M.P., AND MR. W. CROSFIELD, J.P. A well-attended special meeting of the General 'Council of the Warrington Liberal Association was held in the Committee-room of the Liberal Club, Bewsey-street, an Wednesday evening, when the chair was taken by the member for the borough, Mr. J. G. McMinnies. Amongst those also present were—Messrs. W. Crostield, J.P., Liberal candidate for the borough, C. Broadbent, J.P., E. J. Guest, J.P., Dr. Gornall, J.P., F. Roberts, J. Walker, F. Dignum, W. Perry, H. Whitham, W. Stirrup, S. Barlow, and H. Roberts (secretary.) 4 letter was read from Mr. John Crosfield excusing his absence in consequence of the death of his friend and relative, Mr. George Fell. Mr. F. Monks wrote regretting his inability to be present. Referring to the agenda of the meet- ing, Mr. Monks wrote that he was glad some action was being taken to give Mr.. Gladstone support and assure him of the confidence we had in him. He hoped also that they would not overlook their own veteran, Mr. McMinnies, and that they would assure him of their unabated confidence in him as their local leader, whose usefulness to the party would not be lessened by his retirement from the din of Parliamentary obstructionists. (Applause.) Mr: Armitage also wrote expressing regret at not being able to attend. several communications were received from :the National Liberal Federation and the City of London Liberal Association, and, having been read, it was decided that the Secretary acknowledge receipt of them. Mr. H. WHITHAM, in accordance with notice, moved " That this meeting heartily apvves of the _ _ -
LIBEI

bill introduced by Mr. Je—sse Collings, for the removal of the disabilities caused by the receipt of medical relief;.and authorises the chairman to sign a petition in favour thereof to the House of Com- mons." The measure for the assimilation of the county and borough franchise had met with great opposition from the Conservative party, by whom we were told that the country did not want the measure. They as borough voters remembered that, they were in the same position as the county re- presentatives were, and it waScharged against them that they were not fit to have the vote, but he thought that now the coutitir was no worse off than . .

At Warrington Borough Court, on Tuesday, Richd. Spann, formerly a wheelwright, of Friars-green, was brought up on remand and charged before Cpun- cillors Greening and Broadbent with having, on the 4.th March, within four months of the presentation of his bankruptcy petition, unlawfully and fraudulently removed divers of his goods to the value of £ to and upwards, contrary to sub-section 5, section it, of the Debtors' Act, 1869 ; with having concealed part of his property to the value of Xi° or upwards, and with having made a material omission in his statement of his affairs.—Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence, and the case for the prosecution was conducted by Mr. P. Davies, instructed bit the Treasury, who de- tailed the main features of the case, as previously made public. In conclus7on ho said that if the goods I since found bad gone into the estate, there would have been an ample divi ion for the creditors. Thy, however, were at that time satiefied that the bank - rupt'e statement was a correct one, and therefore he escaped with a composition of 45 in the £ That was thefraud for which the Bench were asked to commit the prisoner.—Witnesses were then Tilled. Mr. E. J. Nicholson, registrar of Warrington County Court, produced the file of the bankruptcy proceedings. The petiiiou was filed on the sth Mar, h, 1885, and a receiving order was made the same day. On the 6th an order of adjudication was made. Prisoner's statement of affairs was made and sworn on the 9th March before the official receiver. The stock-in-trade was stated as—estimated cost, £5O ; to realise £3O. ORMSKIRIC v. WARRINGTost.—This match was played at Warrington on Siturday,,and although five of the first team were absent from the home eleven, the visitors were completely defeated. Ormskirk won the toss, anti elected to bat on the good wicket prepared for the match. W. Stretch played steadily, but was snapped at the wicket by Fair. dough. James and T. Ainscough were dismissed, and the hopes of Ormskirk were somewhat damped. The fourth and fifth wickets fell without adding to the total. J. C. Lawton had bowled finely up to this time, sending down five oyers for four wickets and twelve runs. He unfortunately sprained his foot, but continued, bowling. H. Ainscough was the only man do make a stand against the bowling. arid was the only double figure scorer. He played confidently, hut was poorly supported, and was bowled last wicket down. Both brothers Lawton bowled successfully, and were ably upheld by smart fielding. The analysis read J. C., 34 runs, 6 wickets, 13 overs, 3 maidens ; C. G., 27 run.s, 4 wickets, 14 overs, 5 maidens. PRESCOT.

2ND LANCASHIRE ST. HELENS ENGINEER VOLUSTTEEBS, PRESCOT COMPANY.-011 Saturday a full dress parade Was held at the headquarters of the newly-formed company, Market-place. Between fifty and sixty mustered under Captain and Adjutant Cords. There were also present Colonel Bothwell and Captain Lyon. Thirty members of the Huyton company marched with their band and took part in the battalion drill in charge of Corpo.al Drill In- structor Stevens and company Sergeant Wainwright. PRESCOT HIGHWAY ROARD.-1 be monthly meeting of this Board should have been held on Tuesday forenoon, but owing to the absence of a quorum no meeting could he held. The only members present were Mr. W. L. Evans (chair- man), Mr. Tyrer, along with Mr. H. Cross (clerk), Mr. W. Goldsworth (surveyor), and Mr. Cowherd (assistant clerk). —Surveyor's Expenditure : The eurve, or's expenditure for the five weeks ending July 2nd was as follows Bold, £ll I Se; Knowsley, £l3 78 7d ; Whisten, 19e ; Rainhill, .£6 44 2d; team labour, £32 14a 50 • new materials, £44 Ns 9d; incidentals,. £1312s 9d; total, £l3l Os SP. ROBBERY AT WOOLTON. Before Messrs. A.. R. Glad- stone and H. Bright, at the Preecot Petty Sessions, on Tues- day. Edward Lot tus, a middle-aged man, was charged with stealing a pot of jam and 3i ounces of tobacco from the shop of Mr. James Ashe, grocer, 24, Woolton-street, Woot- ton, on the 3rd inst. The prisoner was seen in Mr. Ashe's shop, and Mrs Ashe noticed something bulky in his posses- sion. She found a pot of jam in his pocket and he Was given into custody. When being searched by P.C. Carl- ton, the tobacco was found in his pos,v salon. Superinten- dent Barker gave the prisoner a very bad character, and the , prisoner was committed for one month with hrud labour. I PRESCOT POLLU.G DISTRICT, ORM,KIRIC DIVISION.—A meeting was held at the Liberal Club. Market place, on Friday evening, for the purpose of electing 28 representa- tives to form the General C mncil for the district. The large reading-room was well filled. Amongst those present were. Messrs. 'F. P. Hewitt, president of the club ; W. Tyrer, T. D. McKenzie, W. G. Scales, J. Pratt, J. Howard, 3. Lawrenson (hon. sec.), A. Appleton, &s.—On the motion of Mr. Lawrenson, Mr. Hewitt took the chair. The names of 23 were submitted and agreed to, hut as no one appeared from the neighbourhood of Knowsley and Croxteth, which are included in the Present polling district, through no copies of -the notice calling the meeting having been sent. there, it was deemed advisable to adjourn the meeting, leav- ing five vacancies to be filled up. , PRESCOT BCARD OF GIJARDIANS.—The fortnightly meet- ing of this tabard was held on Thurseay at the Workhouse, Whiston, near Prescot.—Mr. Newsome called attention to the inferior quality of the milk which had recently been supplied to the house.—lt was decided that the clerk should inform the contractor that in the absence of improvement the contract would be cancelled.—On the recommendation of the Building Committee, the sum of £l5O was voted to Mr. Sumner, architect, of, Liverpool, for professional ser- vices rendered in connection with the proposed erection of vagrant wards, dm. Mr. Thomas Roberts, builder, North- street, St. Helens, was recommended by the Building Com- mittee as the contractor for the works, his tender being £3,27o.—The minutes were confirmed.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board asking for further in- formation with regard to the sinking of a well at the Work- house, and enclosing copies of letters received from Mr.l Berry, hon. secretary of the Prescot Ratepayers' Asso- ciation, and the Rev. Thomas Chambers, a Guardian, both of whom protested against the expenditure M £BOO for sinking a well, when an adequate supply might be ob- tained from Mr. Longton.—The Clerk was instructed to in- form the Local Government Board that the Guardians had no observations to make on the matter.-1 he number of in- mates this week was reported as 406 ; last week, 417; cor- responding period of last year, 389. It was stated that orders had been issued by the Local Government Board au- thorising the election of a guardian for the township of Eccleston in the place of Mr. John Fidler. deceased, and a guardian for the township of Ralohill in the place of Mr. A. Meadows, resigned.
The Queen held a Council at Windsor ol Thursday after- noon. Lord Cranbrook, Sir Francis Sandford, Sir Massey Lopes, and Sir Henry Fletcher left London by special train to attend.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, THURSDAY. When Lord Salisbury demanded of Mr. Gladstone that he should give himself and the Liberal party up, dad hand and foot, for -what remained of the session, the extraordinary request was formally re- fused. The Marquis, making a virtue of the accept- ance of the office for which he and his friends had during three years incessantly schemed and plotted, declared that he could not carry on the Queen's Government unless Mr. Gladstone would promise in advance to support him. Failing to obtain such a pledge, Lord Salisbury took office and has found,all his fears of obstruction illusory. Never in modern Parliamentary' days has public business advanced by such leaps and bounds as during the past week. At one sitting thirty-four votes in,the Civil Service Estimates were finished clean off. Mr. Mundella in his speech at Sheffield has explained this pheno- menon in a single sentence. Public business is going forward rapidly in the House of Commons, because all the principal obstructionists are on the Treasury Bench. The Fourth party is absolutely non-existent, and Mr. Ashmead Bartlett's• mouth is closed by the bestowal of a small and comically incongruous office. As for the Parnellites, they have been bought off at what some of the Conservatives regard as a criminally heavy price. What Mr. Chamberlain and Sir Charles Dilke failed to induce the maprity of the Liberal Cabinet to essay, a Tory Cabinet has swallowed at a gulp, and the experiment of govern- ing Ireland by the common law will forthwith be

wide. The Conservatives are, naturally enough, much surprised at the turn affairs have taken in the House of Commons. But, party faction aside, the state of things is one upon which the public may be congratulated. It does not necessarily follow that because votes in supply are passed at the rate of twenty or thirty a night therefore the Work is being scamped. What used to take place when the Liberal Government was in power was not of the nature of inquiry or discussion; it was simply ob- struction. If there is anything wrong or suspicious about a vote it can be talked of, and if 'necessary divided upon within the space of an hour. Take the standing scandal of the royal yachts, for ex- ample. There is the Victoria and Albert, one of five yachts at the service of her Majesty, but which is not used more than twice in ten years. It is now being re-decorated for use in bringing over some of the royal guests to the approaching wedding of Prince Henry of Battenberg with the Princess Beatrice. The yacht originally 'cost £200,000. £56,000 has been expended upon repairs only last year, and now a further sum of £3,000 was asked for, an incidental addition to the large sums already voted on account of the wedding. Such an arrangement is absolutely indefensible. There is no question here of restticting the conve- niences of her Majesty. It is simply the case of a useless and costly appendage which the taxpayer is asked to keep up. In a very ;brief speech Mr. Labouchere called .attention to the matter. Lord George Hamilton made some. commonplace official excu,Se, a division took place, and the whole matter was over in twenty-five minutes. It was obviously hopeless from the first to obtain an immediate re- ,form. The conclusion of the division was foregone. Nevertheless public service was done by calling at- tention to the matter, and it cannot be said that the time of the House was unduly wasted. It is the same with all other questions that come up in Committee of Supply. If obstruction is designed, conversation can be indefinitely prolonged. If busi- ness is meant half an hour or an hour sutaces, and progress may be steadily, even rapidly, made. The Conservatives are already pluming themselves on this state of things, and will doubtless in a week or so, certainly before the general election, begin to represent that all this is due to their better man- agement of affairs. To be able to make this asser- tion they must forget Lord Randolph Churchill's almost abject acknowledgment on Monday night of Mr. Gladstone's "considerate, even magnanim- ous" treatment of the Government. The fact is, Mr. Gladstone is more than ever master of the House of Commons, and the influence of the majority, quietly exercised, is practically unques- tioned. Sir Michael Beach and his colleagues sit on the Treasury bench on sufferance. As long as they are tractable and follow closely on the lines laid down by their predecessors things will go smoothly. One step to the right' or to the left will instantly bring upon their shoulders the restraining hand of the leader of the Opposition. Mr. Gladstone is pretty constantly in attendance, hut happily does not now find the necessity of re- maining till the early hours of the morning. His health has vastly improved, and with it his spirits. He evidently enjoys the comparative quietude, and above all the rare experience of respectful treat- ment which he now Bleep at the hands of the Con- servatives. Lord Hartington is thoroughly enjoy- ing himself—that is to say he keeps away from the lait.4e of Commons. Mr. Chamberlain and Sir Charles Dilke are constantly in attendance, but like Brer Rabbit "lie low and say nothing." Sir Michael Beach is a shade more (gloomy. Lord Randolph, on Monday, when he took his seat on the Ministerial bench, selected a modest position at the remote end, but before the sitting was over he had moved up, dispossessed Mr. W. H. Smith of his seat on the left of Sir Michael Beach, and formally assumed his _natural position as joint leader of the House. The energies of a considerable section of members of the House of Commons are at the present mo- ment concentrated upon an object outside the ordinary range of practical politics. It has nothing to do with Afghanistan, Egypt, India, or even Ire- land. Its nearest approach to domestic politics is that it is closely connected with the redistribution of seats. The Yemenites, as is well known, have persevered in their original plan of remaining in the places they have hitherto tilled, independent of ,the change of Ministry. Their theory is that the politics of English parties are nothing to them. Whether Mr. Gladstone is in and Lord Salisbury rout, or whether Lord Salisbury is in and Mr. Glad- stone out are alternatives to which their great Minds are absolutely indifferent. Political Vicars of Bray, whatever happens, they retain their seats below the gangway on the left of the Speaker. This in ordinary times would actually serve the conve- nience of the House, though that is certainly not the motive ot the Parriellites. But in the present extraordinary circumstances, when the majority are in Opposition, the presence of thirty or forty Irish- men below the gangway is a, serious matter. What happens every day now is a series of strategic ineve- merits, by which the Radicals and Parnellites attempt to secure corner seats. At first Mr. Potter, I Mr. Dillwyn, and Mr. John Morley took the Par- nellites by surprise, and day after day secured the -seats hitherto sacred to the presence of Mr. Healy and Mr. Sexton. Now the Parnellites have wakened up. The Radicals come down early; but the Irish members are earlier, and during this week the Irish- men have generally won. The Radicals are, how- ever, not defeated, and the contest is daily renewed with unflagging activity and spirit. It is difficult to say how the affairs of Europe have been carried on during the pat week. It s well known they are directed from Paris by M. de Blowitz, the famous correspondent of the Times. •But Mr. Blowitz, like' commoner men, sometimes yearns for a holiday, and he has taken a whole week in London. I met him the other night, and was at once impelled to ask who he might be. He -certainly is one of the most remarkable looking in- dividuals on the face Of the earth. His height does not exceed five feet, whilst he is so broad shouldered and large in the limb that, as far as height is con- cerned, it would appear almost immaterial whether he was lying on his side or standing on his feet. His head is of colossal proportions, and presents a sudden oval flash of baldness amid a thick fringe of blue black hair. He has a red face shining forth through a thicket of black whisker and beard. His manner is founded upon traditions of Louis Quatorze, though the effect when he bows and gracionslywaves his hand is, perhaps,not quite equal to that wielded by the Tate monarch. Mr. Blowitz speaks English after a kind, with a guttural accent that seems to indicate German birth. As a matter of fact the great man is a, Polish Jew. I forget is real name, though it certainly is not Blowitz. That is the name of his natal village, which he took on as some of the old Scottish lairds •are known by the name of their territorial patri- mony. Whilst here for a period only too brief, M. Blowitz has been lionised to his heart's content. Everybody laughs at him, but everybody talks to him and asks him to dinner, or, as Lord Rosebery did, to a more prolonged visit in country quarters. Meanwhile Prince Bismarck, the French Govern- ment, the Czar, Italy, and the Xing of Spain have been left to look after themselves. Owing to the many Ministerial appointments, new *peerages, and elections and re-elections which have attended upon the formation of the Salisbury Adtainistration, the editor of " Dod's Parliamentary Companion" is taking the unusual step of prepar- ing a second edition of that time-honoured record, which will be immediately forthcoming. As there will be embodied in this practically all the last elections under the system remodelled in 1832, and slightly revised in 1867, the book will have the

value of a historical document, and as such will be frequently consulted in coming years by those who wish to see how matters were managed in days when small boroughs Were still existing and tolera- ted. But it may be suggested to the successor of the venerable but departed Mr. Dod that in order to give confidence to the future reader the glaring errors which disfigure the edition for 1585 must be corrected. There is really no excuse for mistakes in a work of this kind; and the editor of "Dod" must exercise more vigilance than has been customary of recent years if he wishes to maintain his work at the high level of its old reputation. It may arise from patriotic bias, but, if anything is to be gathered from conversations overheard on the terraces of the Inventions Exhibition, it is a very general opinion that the Executive Council do not deserve any lavish thanks for bringing over at great expense a series of German bands for the delectation of the public. Those who know any- thing of the English military bands feel certain that the people who flock to the Exhibition would be better pleased with the efforts of their own country- men than with those of the ever-present Teuton. It may be hoped that next year the Council will be forced by a rapidly-growing public opinion to see , matters in the same light.

Sir,—Could something not be done to regulate the vehicular traffic at the bottom of Bridge-street? In ordin- ary times the confusion there is bad enoagh, bat now that the very ratan capacity of the street is occasionally made less by the carrying Out of the improvements, there is im- minent danger of some very serious collision taking place. As for foot passengers, their only safety lies in judicious dodging. I should think the presence of an intalligent con- stable would go a long waY towards bringing about a b, tter state of things, and more particululv If he kept a restrain- ing hood upon those JAhus who seem to have so strong an inclination to show off the paces of their animals. A EIGHT-OF-WAY QUESTION. • Sir,—A friend of mine took a walk a few days ago through the Arpley footpaths and across Walton Arches, intendiny• to cross Morley Common to Lower Walton. But on arriving at the Common he found the pathway barri- caded, and also guarded by a It.ipper of Sir Gilbert Greenell's. who informed him that there was now no road. Can you inform your readers whether Sir Gilb,rt has any right to take possession of the Common and stop an ancient footpath, I presume, for game preserving purposes? The baronet of Walton Hall seems to care more for the votes than for the rights of the men of Warrington. It is titus the matter was looked intl.—Y.urs.cte., A MEMBER OF THE OLD FOOTPATH SOCIETY.

P. 8.—1 enclose my card. [lf the footpath has by use been dedicated to the public, the landowner cannot stop it. Perhaps some of our readers living in Walton will be able to say bow long the footpath iu question has bPen used,—ED. Ex.]

"STOPPAGE OF THE FOOTPATH ACROSS TLIE MESNES." Sir,—This was the heading of a communication which appeared in your last issue, and which was signed by that übiquitous and mysterious " A Ratepayer." If the author of the epistle fancies his outpourings have weight and an ap- pearance of authority because "A Ratepayer" appears as the writer, he is sadly in error. Bath " weight" and "authority " are conspicuous by their absence from the letter in question. I presume he is the same " Ratepayer " who formerly addressed you; for I have in vain looked for another " Ratepayer " who manifests the least inte:est in what " Ratepayer" describes "as the rights of the public in this matter." Ido not know whether Ratepayer "is prompted by personal spite, or whether his ruling passion is that " green-eyed monster," jealously; probably there is a mixture of both, and that will account for "A Ratepayer" seeking refuge under a signature which may mean any one of the hundreds of ratepayers in this district. His advice as to the course the C onmissioners should pursue in the mat- ter is ridiculously amusing, and for his credit's sake, it 'is well the writer gives no other means of identification I than that of " A Ratepayer." He even develops into " in- timidation " by covertly exhorting "our prospective mem- ber" to move in the matter. But his impudence is only equalled by the unblushing effrontery with which he as authoritatively asserta "the road is and has been unques- tionably a public road." It has never been proved to be a public road; on the contr. Irv, there is evidence to prove that It is not a public road " Ratepayer's" unsupported asser- tions and opinion 4 will not be taken for facts, and his accu- sation against Mr. Fairclough, who, he says, " has acted very inconsistently," is as unfounded as it is illogical. Mr. Fairclough is the only member of the Board of Commis- sioners who hoe acted truly consistent, and Mr. FAirclough's remark at a recent meeting that people make abort cuts " across a ptiyet.l field for a year or two, and then, forsooth. they claim it as a public road, appeare to be trite in this case. No doubt the Commissioners know more about the so-called "public footpath" than "A Ratepayer," and if the latter thinks that the local authority should spend an unlimited amount in rash illegal proceedings for the ' benefit of a spiteful and jealous few, who can be counted on the fingers of one band, he is evidently troacquinted with the public duties of the Board. I venture to assert, sir, that not 0n.., in every 100 ratepayers in the township cares a fig shout the so-called "right of way." Indeed, they care no more about it thins they do about the vain cries rot "A Ratepayer."—Yours, Ate., A LOOKEHON. Earlestown, July Btb, 1885. THE NATIONAL -REFORM UNION AT ST.

div.head: HELENS.
div.p: HELENS.

Sir.—l saw in your paper the report of a•meeting of the St. Helens Branch of the National Reform .Union, with an address by the secretary to the Union, Mr. R. C. Richards. It is all very well for discontented palitici sus and crotchet- inong,rs to air their eloquence and outpour their vapoury imaginings at their hole and-corner meetings, in the pre- sence of a select few of their own particular &loins, and then forsooth, proclaim it as a test of the feelings, and an expression of the opinions, of the majority of the inhabi- tants of the town. Mind, sir, lam not saying that this course has been adopted in :it. Helens, but to my mind it looks very mach like it. However straightforward every- thing may be and however industrious and energetic people may be, there are always others, in any body or class of men who fancy they can be more straightforward, and that they can do more and be more energetic thau those who have had any particular task or duty to perform. In fact. sir, there are grumblers in every society, grumblers and faultfinders at everything, and I think such might be con- sidered the case in regard to the St. Helens Branch of the National Reform Union. They eompliin that political education in St. Helens has been neglected hitherto—and though no institution was named, it can easily by guessed that they grumble at the club in Hardshaw-street, which has hitherto existed to disserhinate Liberal principles and ideas among the people of St. Helens. I will not say that that programme has been carried out, but what course do the National Reformers adopt in order to remedy the " evil." I should have thought that they would have actively be- stirred themselves to rouse the old institution from its lethargy, and in a body infuse! new energy and activity into its organisation. But no, that would not suit the would-be popularity seekers. Their "light and learning" would be hid under a bushel ; they must come to the front, and if necessary, throw the old horse" overboard. Ac- cordingly they start a society of their own—they are one

and alfe'ager to do their utrnost to secure its mice -ss, and there is a rivalry as to who shall have the honour of ac- complishing the most in that direction. The first public meeting would appear to have satisfied its "promoters," but has it satisfied the working-men and voters that it was necessary to have such a ..brench," and satisfied them as to its principles, object., and aims? I think not. I shall very probably be one who will possess a vote at the next General Election, and before I give my support to the St. Helens Branch of the Natiowsl Reform Union I should like to know something mere about it.—Yours. dro.,

Slr,—The friends of " law and—orie—r are at last in power. After some desperate efforts in the way of making a bargain, we see them at last seated on the Treasury benches. Could they have bound over Mr. Gledstone and the Liberal party to keep the peace, thee most certainly would have done so ; that is, they would have used the cloture in a fashion most peculiarly Conservative. This not being possible, they have been content to take place without haying power. Their term of office may be short. or it may not ; at all events it will include a number of months, wherein the controlling power of Parliamest will he absent What their policy will be none of Us know. Already we See the high tone of principle characterising Mr. Gladstone's Government is te be deported from, and what was wrong is now to be right. Who &es not remem- ber the monstrous assertions made respecting the so-called Kilmainnim Treaty, that the Government " was aiding and abetting Irish consoiratore, working hand in hand with the 1 spoliators and confiscators of ,property ?" Yet what do we see now? That Same party depeoding, not only in the House of Commons, but throughoet the country, upon the Irish vote The Irish, acting under instructions, curled Tory in for Wakefield. Should the Tories win the General Election, I am sadly afraid the Irish will have mach Cause to regret their blind conq lence in them. 1 I see Mr. Charles Lewis is already taking steps to gather around him a sufficient number of Tory members to enable him to force the Government to ireroduce Concion. No doubt some steps will be taken to stop this, as Government will dread such a course as this at the present time as being inopportune. Mr. Lewis is direc'or of ten joint stock corn- paniee and dreads the Irish National Party. In Egyptian matters the nation may well look with Sus- picion at what seems the probable course events are going to take. Sir Henry D. Wolff, a director of eight jeint stock companies, is appointed to look after, in a more direct fashion than has hitherto been done, the bond-holde-e' in- erests. Connected, as he is, with a large ni mey lending concern, he, and those who act with him, are directly inter- ested in keeping things as they are; the Pellaheen must not expect to firnt a friend in Sir ,H. D. Wolf!. With Russia our connection will be of a most slippery kind. Lord Salisbury's insulting comparison ,will not soon be forgotten, and Lord Randolph Churchill's statement that

With Lord Randolph and a few others of the present Cabinet, anyone who cared to stand by the hard and fast line of consistency might have a nice little dispute. Lord Randolph in October 1883 described the County Franchise as" most unjustifiable, earning from anyone who pretends to be a Conservative," and as his lordship proceeds, he seers to get angryiat the idea of anyone supposing that the addition of "perfectly illiwate ag,icultural labourers to the electorate " will benefit the Conservative cause. In fact his lordship goes so far as to advise his questioner to join the Radicals at once if he is in favour of thr assimila- tion of the County and Borough Franchise. Lord Carnar- von, speaking on the same subject, said "the Bill of 1832 made a change which was mist unsatisfactory; it led to the absolute sweeping away of small boroughs." In 1867 his lordship resigned office, rather than consent to a Reform Bill, and now he says " But I am prepared, in view of the facts of the present day, to recognise the new position in which we are now placed." Exacty so; he and those working and thinking as he does have fought against and hindered all measures of reform until they find themselves beaten. Lord Salisbury was so stupidly ignorant as to the feeling of the country on the franchise question that he siid—n Nobody really cues much about it; nobody prays for it," and he went on to say, 'lt seems to me exceedingly probable that the mea- sure which is to be proposod will be one of a kind th ft will receive very strenuous opposition from the parry to whieh we belong." Now whoa he and his party have found out their mistake they, are anxious to pose as the friends of the people, knowing the truth of Laden Rollin's aLyini, " March without thd people and you march into night." It is but necessary for working-men to look at the compo- sition of the present Ca'binet to be satisfied that little good to them will come from It. Essentially aristocratic, its members kn6w little of the ways or requirements of trade, and should they venture to touch even the fripge of trade questions they will most assuredly burn their fingers. The times are changed. Aristocrats must no longer govern. Lord Clarendon, the Tory historian, speaking of the Cecil from whom the present Prime Micister claims descent says —6, N. act of power was ever proposed which he did not advance and execute with the utmost rigour; no man so great a tyrant in this country.", As the first so will the last be, given the opportunity. .

A TEST ON NATIONAL SOBRlETY.—Teetotallers will be glad to receive from the Lancet the suggestion of an in- fallible test of national temperance. Oar contemporary de- duces the Registrar-General's annual report the conclusion that the eurest way of judging whether temperance is increasing or diminishing is by comparing the mortality front liver Complaint one year with, another. Inordinate consumption of alcohol undoubtedly produces that disease in most cases, the people who can drink, sixty glasses of punch a day without appearing any the worse tieing excep- tions to toe rule. statistics are said to show that liver complaint is especially prevalent among publicans and others whose avocations bring them censtantly into contact with alcoholic temptation, and that by itself aff.ads some confirmation of the theory. Stronger support still is ob- tained on comparing the anuai ret zrns rif mart dity from liver diseases. This reached lts maximum in 1875, when the number of such deaths per each million of the popula- tion amounted to 466. That year. it will be remembered, ended the period when our prosperity bad advanced by "leaps and bounds, " with an accompanying augmentation of wages and drunkenness. The decline in trade began shorty afterwards, and simultaneously the mortality from liver complaint began to decrease, a process which, • has gone on uninterruptedly until the present date.

A WESTON MAN'S DEATH IN THE SttUOAN. The death is announced of George Vernon Tudor, eon of the I ate Mr. James Tudor, chemical engineer, of Weston, late a private in the 20th Hussars, a regiment which per- formed such valuable service in the Sladan. Tudor, who was taken ill on Whit Monday, died at Suez on the 16th June of enteric fever. While in Egypt the youeg soldier wrote several letters of deep interest to his mother, from which much of the sufferings of the brave hearts of Eng- lish soldiers may be learned. With his comrades in arms Tudor was a great favourite, and his high spirit and daring which he displayed in the saddle marked. him as a young fellow of great promise. He was a private in the troop of th. 20th Haasars, and reached Suez on the llth ,March. The heat at that time was almost unendurable to the English soldiers who had just left the cold climate of I England. In one of his letters speaking of water, he says "You do not know the value Of water in England. Here there is little allowed for man and horse, and the poor horses gasp for it long before the watering time arrives." In a letter dated April oth, from Suakin, he says:—" I have been in three engagements, and have not received the slight- est injury. Tudor little dreamt of the fate that WAS awaiting him. After passing through several engagements unscathed, he fell a victim to the fever, and died in the hospital at Suez as stated above. The news that reached his mother was from a comrade—Corporal Allen, B Troop—who in terms of deep and heartfelt sorrow announced the death of 'his friend in the hospital at ••• nee. Allen says he was deeply at- tached to Tudor. The worst of it was that he died some 200 miles from where he was then stationed, and he would have given 20 years of his life to have seen him at the last. The corporal's epistle is a very touchinv composition, and is an indication of the respect in which Tudor was held by his comrades. His early death is much regretted, and great sympathy is felt with Mrs. Tudor, who was only recently left a widow.
ENRIBITION_OF GAS APPLIANCES AT RUNCORN.

-- In Bethesda Lecture Hall On Tuesday morning there com- menced an exhibition of gas appliances for domestic use. This is the third exhibition of this description promoted by the Runcorn Gas Company within the pest few years, their principal object being to encourage the use of gas for cook- ing and heating purposes in the labourer's cottage and the gentleman's mansion. The company possess many testimo- nials from townspeople of the efficiency of gas stoves, and the economy they effect in the household expenses ; so that intending purchasers Are not compelled to rely solely upon the !manufacturers' statements of the qualities and capabili- ties of the appliances they offer. Cooking and heating 'stoves of various designs and all sizes are, therefore, the chief ob- jects on view, and they are supplied by Mr. Thos. Fletcher, of Warrington, and Messrs. Charles Wilson and Sons, Carl- ton Works, Leeds. Each firm occupies nearly one half of the room, and the Gas Company display in the remaining spice a tasteful assortment of chandeliers,globes, hall lamps, and patent burners. A model dry meter ad a model wet meter are also shown. Cooking stoves have been often des- cribed, and both Mr. Fletcher and Messrs. Wilson exhibit a considerable number with many patented improvements. Mr. Fletcher's paddle burners and reyereible grill are a great convenience to the stores he exhibits, while hia heating stoves, with asbestos fibre frond, which give an intense heat for a small consumption ef gas, are handsome in design and appearance. The patent quick washer should commend it- self to the bousewifee; as it is perfectly harmless to the cloth- ing, and it is very effective and economical, both as regards labour and money. The instantaneous water beaters are capital inventions. There is a continuous stream of cold witer entering the cylinder at one paint, and a continuous flow of scalding hot water at another; and by this arrange- ment a large bath can be quickly filled with water of a fitting temperature. Patent coffee roamers, which, the inventor claims, gets the greatest weight of coffee high pressure and other burners, laundry and tailors' stoves, bath heaters. smoothing iron heaters, and a ; variety of other appliances are on view. Mr Fletcher has obtained several gold medals by the excellency of his inventions. Aunoragst Messrs. Wil- sons' stock may be singled cut the "Eclipse "cooking stove, ' by which a dinner for a family may be cooked for less than a penny, and a stove constructed to take the place of the kitchen ranee, one whieh the inventors claim numerous ad- ' vantages. The breakfast cooker is a neat and handy arrange- merit. By its means breakfaet with toast, chops, steaks, or bacon, can be prepared in ten minutes; water being boiled at the same time the edibles are teeing cooked. A large bath occupies a prominent place. With the cohsamption of 20 feet of gas, which in Runcorn would coat three fartbinge, 20 gallons of water can be heated in the bath in $0 minutes.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.. HOUSE OF LORDS.

The House met at four O'clock. MISCELLANEOII9.—E4rI NORTHBROOK called attention to Certain statements relative to the Admiralty esqmates made in the House of Commons last night by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. These statements were based on misconcep- tion, and the noble Eat gave notice to call attention to the subject on Tuesday.—The Duke of ARGYLL called attention to the circumstances attending the recent change of Ad- ministration and the effect on the political prospects of the country. Wan regard to foreign affairs and the general ' election pending in four mouths, it was impossible for the Prime Minister to speak with firmness, and with ! regard to domestic politics there was no one to wham I the people could turn for guidance. The debate collapsed after some remarks from Lord Rosebery and Lord Truro.—Lord Hettnis then moved the second reading of the East India Loan of T,n Millions Bill.. His lordship explained the various purposes for which the , loan was needed. Earl KIMBERLEY supported the Bill, which was read a second time wittaout discussion.—Earl Bhstrcimun, replying to Lord Braye, said that on Monday the House would be informed what steps the Govirnmenr would take with reference to the Criminal Law Amendment Bill.
T-• he House then adjourned. OF COMMONS. HOUSE COMMONS.

The House met at fur o.clock. QUEsTioNs.—Lord J. MANNERS, replying to Mr. S. Leighton , admitted the desirability of increased amounts that might be deposited in Post Office Savings' Banks, but there would not be lime during the present session to deal with the subject.—Slr R. CROSS, replying to Mr. A. Grey, said the orders to the police were to use their utmost efforts to suppress vice. The Criminal Law Amendment Bill would, he thought, be sufficient to bring offenders to j ant ice.—Lord G. HAMILTON, replying to a question. said it was intended to institute an inquiry into the Admiralty expenditure.—Lord R. CHURCHILL, replying to Mr. Buchanan, said ho adhered to the opiaion that he had ex- pressed. that an inquiry into tho Glvernment of India Act was absolutely necksa try. He spoke his individual opinion. The Government had not yet,,had time to consider the sub- ject.—Mr. W. H. SMITH, replying to Mr. H. McCarthy, said no communications had passed between the Govern- ment and Captain Wilson with respect to a proclamation alleged to have been issued by that officer for the capture of Oliver Pain, dead or alive. The CaawcaLLott of the EXCHEQUER announced that the Government having determined to deal with the subject of medical relief disqualification, on Monday a bill would be introduced on the subject. _Mr. Marriott took his seat on re-slection for Brighton.

DESTITTJTION AND Or -Mr. S. SMITH called the attention of tile House to the extreme destitution and over- crowding in our great cities, especially amompt the class of unskilled casual labourers, and ,noved that it was expedient to establish a system of compulsory industrial training for children between twelve and sixteen years of age,in order to

tr. them to earn their own living at home and in the colonies The subject, he said, was one of vest social importance, and they had abundant evidence of toe fact of overcrowding of late years, especially in the report of the Commission for Housing the Poor. One of the meet important circum• etances brought out by the investigation was the large number of whole families now living in one room. It ap- peared that there were sixty thousand families representing three hundreil thousand persona so loeged, and this led beth to moral corruption and bad the most serious physical effects. He said he had deeply thr ught over the question, and he came to the conclusion that induetriel train- ing was the best way Af dealing with the admitted evil. He suggested the establishment of night schools, at which at- tendance etionld be compulsory, and thought the boys should be taught bontmalting, carpentering, printing, and other easily acquired trades, and thought the girls should be instructed in sewing, laundry work, cooking, and other employments suitable to women, and if this were done he felt the eising generation would be better able to cope with foreigners than they were at present. He was of opinion that the present brain work in our ele- :neotary schools was excessive, and if they educated the hand, eye, and arm more than they bad done the best reeults would follow. He strongly appealed to the House to pass the resolution.—Profe.ssor &meter seconded the resolution, and warmly advocated the establishment of the schools sug.
