Mae. DUDLEY IN THE ASYLIEC—Mrs Dudley is now confined in the intermediate ward at Middleton Asylum. Her apartment measures sevmteen feet by fourteen ; it is lofty, well ventilated, and affords a delivhf ful view of farms, groves of trees, hills, towns for thirty miles. It contains two beds, and Mrs Dudley's companion is a handsome giil, who imagines herself to be the only daughter of Qoeen Victoria, and the Supreme Coinininder of the crack regi- ment of New York, the gaventh. Mrs Dudley will be speedily transferred to the convalescent ward, and her release is spoken of as a matter of weeks rather than months.

DROWNING.—FATAL ATTEMPT AT RESCUE —oo. Saturday evenine, near Pendlebury, Peter Horton, 13 years of age. was playing at the edge of the Irwelt with several other boys when he fell into the river. The screams of the other boys was heard by an artist named Charles Billingten, 19 years old, who was sketching, and he immediately went to the boy's rescue, but he was unfortunately drowned in his eraimeworthy attempt to rescue 'the boy.—On Saterthy John F. Crowley, aged eight years, Was getherine tl mere on the banks of the Bridgewater Camil at Westwood, neer Woreley, when he overbalanced himself and fell into the water and was drowned. SQUABBLE BETWEEN MARRIED WOMEN.—Before Mr. A. R. Gladstone and H. Bright, at the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, Elizabeth Woodward, a married woman, was summoned for assaulting Emma Jane Bradshaw, on the 30th June, and also for using defamatory language con- cerning. Alice Atkinson ; and the Woman BEVinhaW Wl9 summoned for using defamatory language to the defendant Wood ward. Mr. Mackenzie appeared for Mrs. B-adshaw and Mrs. Atkinson. It appeared that on the evening of the 30th ult. Mrs A,kinson had occesion to visit her mother's house, and when she was returning she passed the defend- ant's house, in Holme's-buildines, Sr. Helens-road. Some words ensued between them as to a pair of clogs, and Mrs. Woodward called Mrs. Atkinson bad names. At that moment Mrs. Bradshaw came up, and Mrs. Wooiward neat foul and threatenine language to her. She also struck Mrs. Bradshaw a severe blow on the meutle—The defendant Mrs. Woodward denied the alleged aesetelt, and accused i Bradshaw of having used abusive and insulting I ingu tee to her.—Mrs. Woodward Was ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for six months for using bed language ti I Mrs. Bredshaw. The other summonses were dismissed. THE BISHOP OF MANCHESTER ON DEMEANOUR TO 4; IN- FERIORS "—The Bishop of Manchester preached on Sunday morning in St. Mary Abbot's Church, South Kensington. His lordship dealt upon copsiderateness towards inferiors, and specially towards servants, as a Christian gems. He said he was sometimes surprised as well as pained to ob- , serve how little the convenience of such persons as servants, governesses, and tradesmen was considered by many in the laying down of plans. His lordship touched upon the paulance of temper which if the slightest thing went wrong, was aroused even in some sweet creatures wham oae might never suspect of such displays of temper. Yet it was per- haps a mere accident which placed us high and others low. which authorised us to speak and obliged them to hear, which subjected human beings, with hearts perhaps as tender as our own, to wanton caprices and the wayward desires of luxuri- ous ennui. Everybody was little to the misfor- tune of getting a bad servant now and then ; hut if ever he heard persons complaining of servants as a class, and saving it was impossible to get good and trustworthy ones, he generally drew the conclusion." You are a bad master or a bad mistress." VIOLENT ASSAULT AT WOOLTON.—At Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday, before Messrs. A. R. Gladstone and H. Bright, a rough-looking fellow named Stephen Ilson' a dock labourer, at Gersten, era charged with unlewfully wounding an Ad man named William Grace, a grocer and hardware dealer, at Woolton.—Saperintendent Barker said the prosecutor was walaing quietly down Quarry street, Wootton, on the previous Friday afternoon, when the pri- soner tan behind him and without the least provocation struck him deliberately a violent blow on the right ear. The prisoner had a very bad character, and he asked that he might be committed for trial. He bad bees several times convicted for assault.—William Grace, the prosecutor, was then called. He stated that he never spoke to the prisoner, and never knew him before the assault WAS committed. His ear was cat and bled very much. He was afterwards at- tended by De Chisholme.—Dr. Chisholme deposed that he found the prosecuter's right ear swollen and very much disenlonred. Behind it was a rugged, lacerated wound, which must have been caused by a severe blow.—P.o Carl- ton said be witnessed the assault. He was in plain clothes at the time, and he apprehended the prbmner. He became very violent, and struck him on the chest with his fist. He also kicked him on the legs. When the handcuffs were put on he bit witness en the right hand. Witness Was compelled to get the assistance of several persons to convey the pri- soner to the police office.—He was committed for trial at the next Quarter Sessions. AN EXTRAORDINARY ELOPEMENT. A Warwickshire elopement, which recently caused a considerable sensation, has just had what may be regarded as a very eatiefactory sequel. Ahout three months since the wife of a Birming- ham manufacturer living at Moseley eloped with a travel- ler of a Birmingham firm. The runaway pair engaged apartments at the Saracen's Head, Shirley, where they staved several days, when an unexpected Incident caused their hurried departure. Some friends of the husband hay- ing ascertained the whereabouts of the couple they awaited one morning near the Saracen's Head, where the Lotherie soon appeared in a trap. He was, however, immediately removed from the vehicle, and notwithstanding his screams and struggles, he was placed full length in the horse-trough, which was full of water. Besides this, the unfortunate young man was pumped on, and finally crowned with a bucket of oatmeal, the bucket being held over his face for a minute or two. Eventually the drenched individual Was allowed to drive away with a friend, minus his hat, collar, cuffs, and necktie. The lady, who witnessed the proceed- ings, was greatly alarmed at the treatment of the partner of her flight ; and in reply to her inquiries, she was assured that she would not he in any way molested. She thereupon packed up her luggage and drove to the residence of some friends. The husband took proceedings for a divorce and was successful, there being no defence. The lade had meanwhile discarded he temporary lover, and Was on Friday remarried to her late husband at Solihull Parish Church.

CLIFTON HALL COLLIERY EXPLOSION.—The coroner's inquiry into the explosion of the Clifton Hall Colliery was continued on Wednesday. Mr. Dickson. Her Majesty's In- spector of Mines, quoted figures showing that in the 34 years ending 1884, of 36,094 deaths by colliery accidents, 7,959 were from explosions and 14,307 ware caused by falls of roofs. The fatalities in the latter category were always less when naked lights were used, snd candles had been used in preference to safety" lamps at Chilton Hall Colliery because the proprietors thought the number of casualties would be lower under this plan. Mr. Martin, Assistant Inspect o: of Mines, said that if the beet kind of " safety " lamps had been used the explosion in all pro- bability would not have taken place. Mr. Hall said that when he was appointed manager lie desired to substitute lamps for naked lights, but the men threatened to strike. On Thursday the inquiry was concluded. Mr. Jobo Higson. mining engineer, reported as to the result of an investiga- tion he had made, at the instance of the coroner, of the colliery workings. He was, he said, of opinion that the Cause of the explosion was the accumulation of a large body of explosive atmosphere in tbe goaves immediately adjoining the highest bay out of No. 2 level east in tho Trencherbono Mine, which was worked by No. 1 tally, that this explosive air resulted from a general weighting of the roof in. the neighbourhood of the nlagte mentioned, and that it was ignited by a candle. Mr. Higson had so fault to find with the general manzgement of the mine and the ventila- tion, but as regards the use of naked lights he was of opinion that it weal& be uneafe to work with such lights in fatnre. The jury found as their verdict that all the deaths were caused by the explosion of a large quantity of indammable gas, that such gas was ignited by a lighted candle, that its emission was sudden and un- expected, that no person was either criminally or censor. ably " to blame, and that therefore the several deceased Persons came te/their death by accident. In view of the diversity of opinion as to,the use of naked lights in mines where explosive gas is known to exitat the jury declined to sly anything as to the propriety of discontinuing such use, but recommended that the practice of using open lights should without loss of time form the subject of inquiry by skilful and experienced persons appointed for that purpose by the Gavernment. The jury also desired very strongly to recommend the appointment of several additional assis tent inspectors of mines, so that a more frequent and thoroagh inspection of the workings within this district may be made.
